UPPPER LIMB
🦾 1. General Overview of the Upper Limb
⭐
The upper limb is designed primarily for mobility, positioning the hand, and performing precise movements.
⭐
Anatomically, it is divided into the pectoral girdle and the free upper limb.
⭐
The pectoral girdle consists mainly of the clavicle and scapula.
⭐
It connects the free upper limb to the axial skeleton and provides a stable but highly mobile base for movements of the arm.
⭐
The free part of the upper limb consists of the arm, forearm, and hand.
⭐
The arm contains the humerus, the forearm contains the radius and ulna, and the hand contains the carpal bones, metacarpals, and phalanges.
⭐
A particularly important anatomical feature is that the upper limb has only one true bony articulation with the axial skeleton:
🔻 The sternoclavicular (SC) joint. 😎
💀
Clavicle is the attached part of the UL.
🔻
The scapula is not directly attached to the thoracic cage by a synovial joint; instead, it is held against the thoracic wall mainly by muscles.
🔻
This arrangement contributes greatly to the remarkable mobility of the upper limb.
🔻
The sternoclavicular joint therefore represents the only direct skeletal connection between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
⭐
The scapula moves over the thoracic wall through a functional articulation often called the scapulothoracic articulation, but this is not a true anatomical joint.
🦴 2. Clavicle
⭐
The clavicle, commonly called the collar bone, is an S-shaped long bone 📏 that acts as a structural strut (A stick or metal bar that keeps something from falling) between the upper limb and the trunk.
🔻
It holds the scapula and upper limb away from the thorax, allowing a wide range of movement.
🔻
The clavicle has a sternal (medial) end, a shaft, and an acromial (lateral) end.
🔻
The sternal end is enlarged (=Larger and round) articulates with the manubrium of the sternum and the first costal cartilage at the sternoclavicular joint. 🔵
🔻
The acromial end is flattened and articulates with the acromion of the scapula at the acromioclavicular (AC) joint.
🔻
The clavicular shaft has characteristic curvature.
⭐
The medial two-thirds are convex anteriorly, whereas the lateral one-third is concave anteriorly (Convex posteriorly). 🫆
⭐
This S-shaped configuration is an important identifying feature of the clavicle.
⭐
The clavicle is unusual because it is a horizontal long bone and is the first bone in the body to begin ossification.
⭐
Most of its ossification occurs by intramembranous ossification, although the medial end develops from an epiphyseal center.
⭐
The clavicle also serves as an important attachment site for muscles and ligaments.
💪
Important muscular attachments include the sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major, deltoid, trapezius, subclavius, and sternohyoid.
⭐
Important ligamentous attachments include the coracoclavicular ligament, consisting of the conoid and trapezoid parts.
⭐
5 differences between Clavicle & Other long bones.
”
1. It lies horizontal.
2.The only long bone having no medullary cavity. 🫆
📝
Note the clavicle is not technically the only long bone that lacks a classic, continuous medullary cavity(=Marrow cavity), as certain small tubular/long bones (such as the individual phalanges of the fingers and toes) also lack a true, prominent marrow cavity and are instead filled with spongy (trabecular) bone interior.
🔖
However, in standard human gross anatomy curricula, the clavicle is uniquely highlighted as the only major or atypical long bone that lacks a true medullary cavity and forms primarily via intramembranous ossification rather than endochondral ossification.
3. Is the first bone to ossify in IUL(〰 fetal life)〰@5th week.
4. Membraneous ossification not cartilagenous.
5.The most commonly fractured bone.
🩺 Clinical Importance of the Clavicle
💥
The clavicle is one of the most commonly fractured bones.
🛡️
The typical fracture occurs near the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, where the bone is relatively weak (=@ the junction of the 2 concavities) 🤯
📝
After fracture, the medial fragment is pulled superiorly by the sternocleidomastoid muscle. 🧠 The lateral fragment tends to move inferiorly and medially, largely because the weight of the upper limb pulls the shoulder downward while the muscular and ligamentous support is disrupted.
⭐
This produces the classic appearance of a drooping shoulder.
▼
The fracture is clinically important because the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus lie posterior/inferior to the clavicle, so displaced fragments can potentially injure these structures.
⭐
Another important point is that the clavicle acts as a force-transmitting strut.
⭐
Forces from the upper limb can be transmitted through the clavicle to the axial skeleton.
⭐ Clavicle Diagrammatic Summary.
⭐⭐⭐
🔻
When the clavicle fractures (usually at the middle/lateral third junction), the fragments are displaced by muscle pull.
○
The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, which attaches to the medial clavicle, pulls the medial fragment superiorly (elevates it).
○
The trapezius muscle normally supports the lateral fragment but is unable to counteract the weight of the upper limb, causing the lateral fragment to droop (shoulder drop).
○
The pectoralis major may also pull the lateral fragment medially.
3. Scapula 🎲
🔻
The scapula is a flat, triangular bone located on the posterolateral thoracic wall.
⭐
It normally extends approximately from the level of the second to the seventh ribs.
⭐
The scapula forms an important component of the pectoral girdle and provides attachment sites for numerous muscles involved in movements and stabilization of the shoulder.
⭐
The scapula has two surfaces, three borders, three angles, and several important processes.
🔻
The posterior surface is divided by the prominent spine of the scapula into two fossae.
⭐
The smaller superior depression is the supraspinous fossa, while the much larger inferior depression is the infraspinous fossa.
⭐
The anterior or costal surface is concave and forms the subscapular fossa.
📌
The subscapularis muscle occupies this fossa.
📋
The scapula has three borders.
📌
The superior border is the shortest and contains the suprascapular notch.
📌
The medial (vertebral) border lies close to the vertebral column,
📌
While the lateral (axillary) border is thicker and extends toward the glenoid cavity.
📋
The scapula has three angles:
📌
The superior angle,
📌
Inferior angle, and
📌
lateral angle.
🔍
The lateral angle is especially important because it contains the glenoid cavity, which articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.
🔖
The scapula also possesses several important processes.
⭐
The spine of the scapula projects posteriorly and continues laterally as the acromion.
🫆
The most palpable lateral part of scapula is acromial process.
⭐
The acromion articulates with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.
⭐
The coracoid process projects anteriorly and serves as an attachment site for several muscles and ligaments.
⭐
Important attachments include the short head of biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, pectoralis minor, and the coracoclavicular ligament.
🤩
High-Yield Scapular Features
🎯
The glenoid cavity is relatively shallow compared with the head of the humerus.
🎯
This provides considerable shoulder mobility but contributes to the susceptibility of the shoulder joint to dislocation.
🎯
The glenoid cavity is deepened by the glenoid labrum, a fibrocartilaginous rim attached around its margin.
⭐
The suprascapular notch is clinically important because the suprascapular nerve passes through the notch, classically passing beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the suprascapular artery usually passes above it.
🧠
A useful memory aid is:
🪖
Army over Navy → Artery over the ligament. Nerve under the ligament.
🟡〰
Suprascapular nerve → UNDER the ligament 🫆
🔴〰
Suprascapular artery → OVER the ligament 🫆
🤹‍♀
Classic mnemonic:
"Army over Navy"
Artery = over
Nerve = under
🎨
At the spinoglenoid notch, the suprascapular nerve passes around the lateral border of the scapular spine to reach the infraspinous fossa.🫆
⭐
The scapula is also essential for scapulohumeral rhythm.During elevation of the arm, movement occurs through coordinated motion at the glenohumeral and scapulothoracic regions.
Clinical Importance of the Scapula
🦽
The scapula provides attachment to the rotator cuff muscles, which stabilize the humeral head in the glenoid cavity.
🤹‍♀
These muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis.
🫟
Injury to the long thoracic nerve, which supplies serratus anterior, can produce winging of the scapula.
🧩
The medial border and inferior angle become prominent, particularly when the patient pushes against a wall.
🧩
The dorsal scapular nerve supplies rhomboid major, rhomboid minor, and levator scapulae, while the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies trapezius.
⭐
Its proximal end consists of the head, anatomical neck, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, and intertubercular sulcus (Bicipital fossa).
🔻
The weakest site of fracture of humerus is surgical neck. 🫆
🎯
Muscles attached to bicipital groove.
👉
The mnemonic for the attachments in the bicipital (intertubercular) groove is
"A lady between two majors."
👸 👨‍✈️ 👨‍✈️
🔹
Lateral lip: Pectoralis Major
🔹
Floor: Latissimus Dorsi ("Lady")
🔹
Medial lip: Teres Major
⭐
The head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula to form the glenohumeral joint.
🤔
The greater tubercle provides attachment for the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor.
🤔
The lesser tubercle provides attachment for subscapularis.
⭐
The intertubercular sulcus, also called the bicipital groove, contains the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii. Kept in the groove by transverse humeral ligament.
⭐
At the distal end, the humerus forms the capitulum, which articulates with the head of the radius, and the trochlea, which articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna.
⭐
The distal humerus also contains the medial and lateral epicondyles.
⭐
The fracture of humerus at medial epicondyle 🦴 Ulnar Nerve damage
🔻
The ulnar nerve passes in a groove directly posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. 🫆
🔻
This superficial and fixed position makes it highly vulnerable to trauma, compression (cubital tunnel syndrome), or fracture of the medial epicondyle. This area is commonly known as the "funny bone."
🔻
Axillary nerve & posterior circumflex humeral artery is at risk with surgical neck fractures.
🔻
Radial nerve is at risk with mid-shaft (spiral groove) fractures producing wrist drop. 🔻 The shaft of the humerus contains the radial groove, through which the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pass.
🔻
Median nerve is at risk with supracondylar fractures.
5. Ulna 😎
⭐
The ulna is one of the two bones of the forearm and lies on the medial side of the forearm in the anatomical position.
⭐
It is the principal stabilizing bone of the forearm at the elbow.
⭐
The proximal ulna is large and forms most of the bony structure of the elbow joint.
⭐
Its major features include the olecranon process, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, and ulnar tuberosity.
🔹
The olecranon process projects posteriorly and forms the prominence of the elbow.
🔹
It receives the insertion of the triceps brachii tendon.
🔹
The coronoid process projects anteriorly and contributes to the trochlear notch.
🔹
The trochlear notch articulates with the trochlea of the humerus.
🔹
The radial notch is located on the lateral side of the proximal ulna, adjacent to the coronoid process.
🔹
It articulates with the head of the radius and forms part of the proximal radioulnar joint.
🔻
The shaft of the ulna is relatively thick proximally and becomes progressively thinner toward the distal end.
🔻
The distal ulna ends in a relatively small head, accompanied by the ulnar styloid process.
🔹 Ulna and the Wrist Joint — High-Yield Point
🔹
A very important exam point is that the ulna does not directly articulate with the carpal bones and therefore does not participate directly in the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.
⭐
Instead, the distal ulna is separated from the carpal bones by the articular disc of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).
🪃
The radius is the principal forearm bone that directly articulates with the proximal carpal row, especially the scaphoid and lunate.
This is a commonly tested distinction:
⭐
Radius → participates directly in the radiocarpal joint.
⭐
Ulna → does not directly participate in the radiocarpal joint.
⚡
The ulna does, however, participate in the distal radioulnar joint, which is essential for pronation and supination of the forearm.
🩺 Important Clinical Correlations of the Ulna
🌤️✨
The proximal ulna is involved in several important elbow injuries.
💥
Fracture of the olecranon can interfere with the action of the triceps brachii and elbow extension.
⭐
The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus rather than through the ulna itself.
💥
Injury in this region can produce sensory symptoms in the medial one-and-a-half digits and weakness of several intrinsic hand muscles.
⭐
The ulna and radius function together during pronation and supination. During these movements, the radius rotates around the relatively more stable ulna.
▼
Exam point
⭐
The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle, producing the characteristic "funny bone" sensation when struck. 🚨
⭐
The ulnar nerve passes in a groove directly posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
⭐
This superficial and fixed position makes it highly vulnerable to trauma, compression (cubital tunnel syndrome), or fracture of the medial epicondyle. This area is commonly known as the "funny bone."
⭐
Axillary nerve is at risk with surgical neck fractures.
⭐
Radial nerve is at risk with mid-shaft (spiral groove) fractures.
⭐
Median nerve is at risk with supracondylar fractures.
2. Radius — Proximal Features
⭐
The radius is the lateral bone of the forearm in the anatomical position, located on the thumb side.
⭐
Compared with the ulna, the radius is relatively smaller proximally but becomes much larger toward its distal end.
⭐
The proximal end of the radius consists mainly of the head, neck, and radial tuberosity.
⚪
The head of the radius is disc-shaped and has two important articulating surfaces.
🔻
Its superior surface is concave and articulates with the capitulum of the humerus.
⬛
This contributes to the humeroradial component of the elbow joint.
🔻
The circumference of the radial head articulates with the radial notch of the ulna and is held against the notch by the annular ligament.
🔻
This articulation forms the proximal radioulnar joint.
🔻
The neck of the radius is the narrow region immediately distal to the head.
🔻
Below the neck is the radial tuberosity, a rough projection that provides the major insertion site for the biceps brachii tendon.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
The radial tuberosity is clinically important because biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity.
🔻
Since the radius rotates during supination, contraction of biceps is particularly effective in supination of the forearm, especially when the elbow is flexed.
3. Arrangement of the Radius and Ulna
🔻
The radius and ulna are positioned parallel to one another when the forearm is in the anatomical position, with the radius lateral and the ulna medial.
🔻
During pronation, the radius crosses over the ulna.
🔻
During supination, the radius and ulna become approximately parallel again.
🔻
The two bones are connected by the interosseous membrane, a strong fibrous sheet extending between their shafts.
🔻
The interosseous membrane provides attachment for muscles, stabilizes the forearm, and helps transmit forces between the radius and ulna.
⭐
High-Yield Movement
↗
Supination → radius and ulna are parallel.
↗
Pronation → radius crosses over the ulna.
This relationship is extremely important for understanding forearm anatomy.
4. Radius — Shaft and Distal End
⭐
The shaft of the radius gradually becomes larger toward the distal end.
⭐
This is the opposite general pattern of the ulna, which becomes smaller distally.
🔻
At the distal end, the radius has several important landmarks.
🎯
The ulnar notch is located on the medial side of the distal radius.
🎯
It articulates with the head of the ulna and forms the distal radioulnar joint.
🎯
The radial styloid process projects distally from the lateral side of the radius. It provides attachment for ligaments around the wrist and serves as an important surface landmark.
🎯
The distal radius also directly participates in the radiocarpal joint, articulating primarily with the scaphoid and lunate.
⭐
Radius Identification
A useful way to identify the radius is:
⭐
Proximal radius = small head
⭐
Distal radius = broad end
⭐
Lateral distal projection = radial styloid
⭐
Medial distal depression = ulnar notch
5. Clinical Correlation — Colles Fracture
⭐
A Colles fracture is a fracture of the distal radius, classically occurring approximately 2–3 cm proximal to the wrist joint.
⭐
The classic mechanism is a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with the wrist in extension/dorsiflexion.
⭐
The distal fragment is displaced dorsally, producing the characteristic "dinner-fork" or "silver-fork" deformity.
⭐
The fracture may be comminuted, meaning the bone is broken into multiple fragments. Associated injury to the ulnar styloid process may occur.
⭐ Colles Fracture — Exam Pattern
”
🧠
Think:
⭐
FOOSH + wrist extension → distal radius fracture → dorsal displacement → dinner-fork deformity.
🆚 Colles vs Smith Fracture
A useful comparison is:
🔴
Colles fracture → dorsal displacement of distal fragment.
🟡
Smith fracture → volar displacement of distal fragment.
🟢
Smith fracture is sometimes described as the reverse Colles fracture.
🩺 Clinical Importance
⭐
Because the distal radius is close to the median nerve and carpal tunnel, significant distal-radius fractures can be associated with median nerve compression and carpal tunnel symptoms.
⭐ "Dinner fork deformity" ⭐
”
🔻
Describes the appearance of a Colles' fracture, which is a complete transverse fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment.
⭐
It is typically caused by a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), resulting in forced dorsiflexion. 🫆
⭐
It is a complete fracture of the distal radius. 🫆
⭐
It is very often associated with an avulsion fracture of the ulnar styloid process. 🫆
⭐
A Colles' fracture is the most common fracture of the distal forearm. 🫆
✨ Hand — 27 Bones
🔻
Each hand contains 27 bones, allowing the hand to perform highly precise and coordinated movements.
🔻
They are divided into:
✨ Carpals — 8
🔻
The carpals are the bones of the wrist.
🔻
They are arranged in two rows of four bones.
🔻
The eight carpals include the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate.
✨ Metacarpals — 5
🔻
The five metacarpals form the framework of the palm.
🔻
They are numbered I–V, beginning with the thumb.
✨ Phalanges — 14
🔻
The phalanges form the fingers.
🔻
The thumb has 2 phalanges:
Proximal + distal
🔻
Each other finger has 3 phalanges:
Proximal + middle + distal
💥
Hand = 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges = 27 bones
🧑‍🏫 Deep Fascia of the Upper Limb
🔻
The deep fascia is a dense connective-tissue layer that surrounds muscles, groups of muscles, vessels, and nerves.
🔻
It provides structural support and helps separate muscles into compartments.
🔻
In the upper limb, important regional parts of the deep fascia include the pectoral fascia, deltoid fascia, axillary fascia, brachial fascia, antebrachial fascia, and palmar fascia.
⭐
The fascia is continuous from one region to another rather than existing as completely separate layers.
3. Pectoral Fascia ⭐⭐⭐
⭐
The pectoral fascia is the deep fascia associated primarily with the pectoralis major muscle.
⭐
It invests the pectoralis major and forms a continuous fascial covering over the anterior thoracic wall. Inferiorly, it becomes continuous with the deep fascia of the anterior abdominal wall. Laterally, as it approaches and passes beyond the lateral border of pectoralis major, it continues into the axillary fascia.
⭐
The pectoral fascia therefore forms part of the continuous fascial system extending between the thorax and upper limb.
⭐ High-Yield Point
”
Think of the relationship as: ”
⭐
Pectoral fascia → ⭐ axillary fascia → ⭐ brachial fascia → ⭐ antebrachial fascia
✅
This represents a continuous fascial system extending along the upper limb.
4. Deltoid Fascia ⭐⭐⭐
🔻
The deltoid fascia is the deep fascia that surrounds the deltoid muscle.
🔻
It forms a strong fascial covering around the muscle and is continuous with neighboring fascial layers.
🔻
The deltoid fascia is important because the deltoid region contains important structures, including the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels, which pass around the surgical neck of the humerus deep to the deltoid.
⭐ Clinical Correlation
”
⭐
An injection given too high or too posteriorly in the deltoid region can potentially injure the axillary nerve.
⭐
The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and provides cutaneous sensation over the skin covering the lower part of the deltoid region through the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
5. Brachial Fascia ⭐⭐⭐
⭐
The brachial fascia is the deep fascia surrounding the arm.
⭐
It forms a cylindrical fascial sheath around the muscles, vessels, and nerves of the arm.
🔻
Proximally, it is continuous with the fascia of the shoulder and axilla.
🔻
Distally, it continues with the antebrachial fascia of the forearm.
⭐
The brachial fascia sends two important extensions inward toward the humerus.
⭐
These are the medial intermuscular septum and lateral intermuscular septum.
⭐
The intermuscular septa attach to the humerus and divide the arm into two major fascial compartments:
⭐⭐
Anterior compartment → primarily flexor muscles
⭐⭐
Posterior compartment → primarily extensor muscles
🔻
This compartmental arrangement is extremely important in anatomy and clinical medicine.
6. Fascial Compartments of the Arm
⭐
The anterior compartment of the arm contains muscles primarily responsible for flexion of the elbow and related movements.
⭐
Its major muscles are:
✓
Biceps brachii
✓
Brachialis
✓
Coracobrachialis
🔻
The main nerve supply is the musculocutaneous nerve.
🔻
The major artery is the brachial artery.
⭐
The posterior compartment of the arm contains the triceps brachii and anconeus, which are primarily involved in extension of the elbow.
🔻
The major nerve supplying this compartment is the radial nerve.
⭐ Exam Pattern
🔻
Anterior arm → flexors → musculocutaneous nerve
🔻
Posterior arm → extensors → radial nerve
This relationship is extremely high-yield.
7. Antebrachial Fascia ⭐
🔻
The antebrachial fascia is the dense deep fascia surrounding the muscles of the forearm.
⭐
It contributes to the organization of the forearm into anterior and posterior compartments and is continuous proximally with the brachial fascia.
⭐
The anterior compartment of the forearm contains mainly flexor and pronator muscles
⭐
While the posterior compartment contains mainly extensor and supinator muscles.
🔻
The antebrachial fascia also becomes thickened at the wrist to form important structures that hold tendons in place.
8. Extensor Retinaculum
⭐
On the posterior aspect of the wrist, the antebrachial fascia thickens to form the extensor retinaculum.
⭐
The extensor retinaculum is a strong fibrous band that holds the extensor tendons close to the wrist.
⭐
Without this retinacular support, the tendons could move away from the wrist during contraction, producing bowstringing.
⭐
The extensor retinaculum forms several osteofibrous compartments through which the extensor tendons pass.
⭐ High-Yield Concept
”
🔻
Extensor retinaculum → posterior wrist → holds extensor tendons in place.
9. Flexor Retinaculum
⭐
Anteriorly at the wrist, the deep fascia becomes thickened to form the flexor retinaculum.
⭐
The flexor retinaculum stretches across the carpal bones and converts the anterior concavity of the carpus into the carpal tunnel.
⭐⭐⭐⭐
The carpal tunnel contains:
⭐⭐⭐⭐
🔻
Median nerve ⭐
🔻
Four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis
🔻
Four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus
🔻
One tendon of flexor pollicis longus
🔻
Therefore, there are nine flexor tendons plus the median nerve within the carpal tunnel.
⭐
The flexor carpi radialis tendon travels through its own compartment associated with the flexor retinaculum rather than through the main carpal tunnel.
⭐
The ulnar nerve and ulnar artery do not pass through the carpal tunnel. They pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal (ulnar canal).
⭐ Clinical Correlation — Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
🔻
Compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome.
🔻
Typical symptoms include pain, numbness, and tingling involving the lateral three and a half digits on the palmar side, although the exact sensory distribution can vary clinically.
⭐
An important anatomical clue is that the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so sensation over the central palm may be relatively spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Palmar Aponeurosis ✅
10. Palmar Fascia and Palmar Aponeurosis
🔻
The deep fascia continues into the palm as the palmar fascia.
⭐
Its central portion becomes markedly thickened to form the palmar aponeurosis.
⭐
The palmar aponeurosis is a strong, triangular sheet of connective tissue located immediately deep to the skin of the palm.
🔻
It has a proximal narrow portion (Apex) that becomes broader distally.
🔻
Distally, it divides into longitudinal bands that extend toward the fingers, particularly toward the bases of digits 2–5.
⭐
The aponeurosis also has transverse fibers that contribute to the structural support of the palm.
🔻
Fibrous septa extend from the palmar aponeurosis into deeper tissues and help divide the palm into functional spaces.
🔻
Fibrous connections also extend toward the skin, helping anchor the palmar skin.
⭐ Functional Importance
”
🔻
The palmar aponeurosis helps:
👉
Protect deeper structures
👉
Anchor the skin of the palm
👉
Improve grip by preventing excessive movement of the skin
👉
Provide attachment and continuity for fascial structures
11. Clinical Importance of the Palmar Aponeurosis ⭐
⭐
A major clinical condition involving the palmar aponeurosis is Dupuytren contracture.
✓
This is a progressive thickening and shortening of the palmar fascia/aponeurosis, producing flexion deformities of the fingers, particularly the ring and little fingers.
⭐
The affected fingers become progressively difficult to extend.
⭐
Exam Association
🔻
Dupuytren contracture → palmar fascia/aponeurosis → flexion contracture of fingers.
12. Cutaneous Innervation of the Upper Limb ⭐
🔻
The skin of the upper limb receives sensory innervation mainly from nerves derived from the brachial plexus.
⭐
However, the skin over the shoulder region receives important contributions from nerves derived from the cervical plexus.
⭐
This distinction is important because not every cutaneous nerve of the upper limb originates from the brachial plexus.⭐
🔻
The upper limb develops as a lateral projection from the embryonic trunk.
🔻
The thumb lies on the preaxial/cranial border of the developing limb.
🔻
This developmental arrangement helps explain the organization of dermatomes and peripheral nerve territories.
13. Dermatomes of the Upper Limb 🌀
⭐
A dermatome is an area of skin supplied predominantly by sensory fibers from a single spinal nerve root.
⭐
Dermatomes are different from peripheral cutaneous nerve territories.
⭐
This distinction is extremely important:
🔻
Dermatome → spinal nerve root
🔻
Peripheral nerve territory → named peripheral nerve
🎯
For example, the thumb is classically associated with the C6 dermatome, while sensory supply to the thumb involves branches of peripheral nerves, especially the median nerve.
14. Important Upper-Limb Dermatomes ⭐
⭐
C4
🔻
The C4 dermatome supplies the skin over the shoulder and lower neck region, particularly around the superior aspect of the shoulder.
⭐
C5
🔻
The C5 dermatome is associated primarily with the lateral upper arm, particularly around the region of the deltoid.
⭐
C6
🔻
The C6 dermatome extends along the lateral forearm toward the thumb.
🎯
The thumb is therefore an important landmark for C6.
⭐
C7
🔻
The C7 dermatome is classically associated with the middle finger.
📝
This is an important correction to a common oversimplification: rather than memorizing C7 as simply "the middle three fingers,"
📌
the middle finger is the classic C7 landmark.
⭐
C8
The C8 dermatome is associated with the little finger and medial side of the hand.
👉
The little finger is therefore an important landmark for C8.
⭐ T1
”
🔻
The T1 dermatome is primarily associated with the medial forearm.
⭐ T2
🔻
The T2 dermatome contributes to sensation around the upper medial arm and axillary region.
🤔
The axilla itself is an important landmark for the upper thoracic dermatomes.
15. ⭐ Classic Dermatome Sequence
📋
For rapid examination review, remember:
🔻
C5 → lateral arm
”
🔻
C6 → thumb
🔻
C7 → middle finger
🔻
C8 → little finger
🔻
T1 → medial forearm
💀
This sequence is particularly useful when interpreting nerve-root lesions, cervical radiculopathy, and neurological examinations.
A simple memory pattern is: ”
6 = thumb
7 = middle finger
8 = little finger
16. Dermatome vs Peripheral Nerve — Very High Yield 🎯
🔻
A dermatome represents sensory distribution from a spinal nerve root, while a named peripheral nerve may contain fibers from multiple spinal nerve roots.
📝
For example, the median nerve carries fibers mainly from C6–T1, while the ulnar nerve carries fibers mainly from C8–T1.
”
📌
Therefore, a patient can have a peripheral nerve lesion or a nerve-root lesion and develop sensory loss in overlapping but not identical areas.
📌
This distinction is fundamental when interpreting neurological examinations.
17. Important Cutaneous Nerves to Know
📋
Several named peripheral nerves are particularly important for upper-limb sensory examination.
🔻
The axillary nerve supplies sensation over the skin covering the lower part of the deltoid region through the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
🔻
The musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying sensation to much of the lateral forearm.
🔻
The radial nerve supplies cutaneous sensation over parts of the posterior arm, posterior forearm, and dorsolateral hand.
🔻
The median nerve supplies important sensory areas of the lateral hand, particularly the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits and corresponding distal dorsal areas.
🔻
The ulnar nerve supplies the medial hand, including the medial one and a half digits.
🔻
The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm supplies much of the medial forearm.
⭐ Important Distinction
”
📌
Do not confuse:
✅
C6 dermatome → thumb
with
✅
Median nerve → major sensory nerve of the lateral hand and thumb-side digits.
✅
They are related anatomically but represent different organizational levels.
⭐⭐ SUPERFICIAL VESSELS, LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE & VENIPUNCTURE OF THE UPPER LIMB
1. Superficial Venous System of the Upper Limb
⭐
The superficial venous system of the upper limb lies within the superficial fascia and is clinically important because these veins are easily visible and accessible for venipuncture, intravenous cannulation, and administration of medications or fluids.
⭐
The major superficial veins are the cephalic vein, basilic vein, median cubital vein, and median antebrachial vein.
⭐
They originate primarily from the venous networks of the hand.
🔹 Dorsal Venous Network of the Hand
🔻
The dorsal venous network is a superficial network of veins located on the dorsum of the hand.
🔻
It receives blood from the superficial veins of the fingers and hand and gives rise mainly to the cephalic vein laterally and the basilic vein medially.
🔻
This arrangement is important to remember because the two major superficial veins of the upper limb can be traced back to the dorsal venous network.
⭐ A useful relationship is
”
🔻
Lateral → Cephalic vein
🔻
Medial → Basilic vein
🔻
The superficial veins communicate extensively with one another, so venous blood can often be redirected through alternative pathways if one vessel becomes compressed or obstructed.
2. Cephalic Vein
🔻
The cephalic vein is the major superficial vein on the lateral side of the upper limb.
🎯
It begins from the lateral part of the dorsal venous network of the hand.
🎯
From the hand, it ascends along the lateral aspect of the forearm and then continues along the anterolateral aspect of the arm.
🎯
At the elbow, it communicates with the basilic venous system through the median cubital vein.
🔻
As the cephalic vein approaches the shoulder, it passes through the deltopectoral groove, which is the groove between the deltoid muscle laterally and the pectoralis major muscle medially.
🎯
It then enters the deltopectoral triangle, also called the clavipectoral triangle.
⭐
The cephalic vein subsequently pierces the clavipectoral fascia and terminates by draining into the axillary vein.
⭐ High-Yield Cephalic Vein Relationships
”
⭐
The most important pathway to memorize is:
🔻 Dorsal venous network → 🔻 Cephalic vein →
🔻 lateral forearm →
🔻 lateral arm →
🔻 deltopectoral groove →
🔻 clavipectoral fascia →
🎯 axillary vein
👉
The cephalic vein is clinically important because it is commonly used for venous access.
👉
It may also be used for insertion of central venous devices because of its relatively direct connection with the axillary vein.
⭐ Important Exam Point
”
⭐
The cephalic vein passes through the deltopectoral groove. This is one of the most commonly tested anatomical relationships.
3. Basilic Vein
⭐
The basilic vein is the major superficial vein on the medial side of the upper limb.
⭐
It begins from the medial part of the dorsal venous network of the hand.
🔻
It ascends along the medial side of the forearm and continues onto the medial aspect of the arm.
🔻
Near the junction of the middle and inferior thirds of the arm, the basilic vein pierces the brachial fascia and enters the deeper compartment of the arm.
⭐
After becoming deep, it ascends alongside the brachial artery and eventually joins the brachial venae comitantes. This union forms the axillary vein.
⭐
Therefore, an important pathway is:
🔻 Dorsal venous network →
🔻 Basilic vein →
🔻 medial forearm →
🔻 medial arm →
🔻 pierces brachial fascia →
🔻 joins brachial veins →
👉 axillary vein
⭐ High-Yield Basilic Vein Point
🔻
The basilic vein is superficial in the forearm and lower part of the arm but becomes deep after piercing the brachial fascia.
🔻
This is an important distinction from the cephalic vein, which remains superficial for most of its course and enters the axillary vein after piercing the clavipectoral fascia.
4. Median Cubital Vein
⭐
The median cubital vein is a short superficial vein 📍 located in the cubital fossa.
✅
It usually connects the cephalic vein laterally with the basilic vein medially.
😎
Its exact anatomical pattern can vary between individuals.
👉
In some people, the median cubital vein forms a relatively direct connection between the cephalic and basilic veins, while other venous patterns may be present.
⭐
The median cubital vein is particularly important clinically because it is the most commonly used vein for routine venipuncture.
🤔 Why Is the Median Cubital Vein Preferred?
✅
It is relatively large, superficial, and usually well fixed, making it easier to access.
🎯
It is also positioned over the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from deeper structures such as the brachial artery and median nerve.
⭐
The bicipital aponeurosis therefore provides an important layer of protection beneath the vein.
🎯 Important Clinical Precaution
👉
The brachial artery and median nerve are deep to the bicipital aponeurosis.
🚫
Incorrect or excessively deep needle placement in the cubital fossa can potentially injure deeper structures.
🔻
Therefore, although the median cubital vein is preferred for venipuncture, proper technique and knowledge of cubital-fossa anatomy are essential.
5. Median Antebrachial Vein
☀️
The median antebrachial vein, also called the median vein of the forearm, is a superficial vein that ascends approximately along the midline of the anterior forearm.
✳️
It lies between the cephalic and basilic venous systems and may drain into the median cubital vein, the basilic vein, or sometimes divide into branches that communicate with both systems.
✳️
Its anatomical pattern is variable, so it is less predictable than the median cubital vein.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
Do not assume that the superficial veins of the upper limb have exactly the same arrangement in every person.
🔻
Venous variation is common, particularly around the cubital fossa.
6. Overall Superficial Venous Pattern
⭐
The major arrangement can be remembered as:
🔻
Dorsal venous network
→ Lateral side: Cephalic vein
→ Medial side: Basilic vein
→ At the cubital fossa: Median cubital vein connects them
→ Cephalic vein → Axillary vein
→ Basilic vein → joins brachial veins → Axillary vein
🔻
The median antebrachial vein runs approximately in the midline of the anterior forearm and communicates variably with the other superficial veins.
6. Overall Superficial Venous Pattern
⭐
The major arrangement can be remembered as:
🔻
Dorsal venous network
→ Lateral side: Cephalic vein
→ Medial side: Basilic vein
→ At the cubital fossa: Median cubital vein connects them
→ Cephalic vein → Axillary vein
→ Basilic vein → joins brachial veins → Axillary vein
🔻
The median antebrachial vein runs approximately in the midline of the anterior forearm and communicates variably with the other superficial veins.
7. Lymphatic Vessels of the Upper Limb
⭐
The lymphatic vessels of the upper limb are divided into superficial and deep lymphatic vessels.
🔻
This distinction is important because the two groups generally follow different anatomical structures.
🔻
Superficial Lymphatic Vessels
🟢
Superficial lymphatic vessels arise from lymphatic networks(plexus) within the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the fingers, palm, and dorsum of the hand.
🟢
They generally ascend through the superficial fascia and travel alongside the superficial veins.
🟢
Lymphatic vessels accompanying the basilic vein generally pass toward the cubital (supratrochlear/epitrochlear) lymph nodes.
🟢
From there, lymph travels toward the lateral/humeral axillary lymph nodes.
🟢
Lymphatic vessels accompanying the cephalic vein generally ascend toward the deltopectoral/infraclavicular lymph nodes and then reach the apical axillary lymph nodes. Some lymphatic vessels may bypass the deltopectoral nodes and drain directly toward the apical axillary nodes.
🎭 High-Yield Relationship
”
A very useful exam association is:
🔻
Superficial lymphatics → follow superficial veins
🔻
Deep lymphatics → follow deep blood vessels
⭐ Deep Lymphatic Vessels
👉
Deep lymphatic vessels accompany the major deep blood vessels of the upper limb, including vessels associated with the radial and ulnar arteries, brachial vessels, and axillary vessels.
🔻
They primarily drain deeper structures such as muscles, joints, and other deep tissues of the upper limb.
⭐
These lymphatic vessels ultimately drain mainly into the humeral (lateral) axillary lymph nodes.
🟢
From the axillary lymph nodes, lymph passes through the other groups of axillary nodes, ultimately reaching the apical axillary lymph nodes and then entering the lymphatic trunks that drain toward the venous system.
8. Axillary Lymph Nodes — Important Context 🟢
🟢
The axillary lymph nodes are commonly grouped into five major groups:
✴️
Pectoral(Anterior)
✴️
Subscapular(Posterior)
✴️
Humeral(Lateral),
✴️
Central, and
✴️
Apical nodes.
⭐
The humeral (lateral) nodes receive much of the lymphatic drainage from the upper limb.
⭐
The pectoral nodes primarily receive lymph from the anterior thoracic wall and much of the breast.
⭐
The subscapular nodes receive lymph from the posterior thoracic wall and scapular region.
⭐
The central nodes receive lymph from the pectoral, subscapular, and humeral groups.
⭐
The apical nodes receive lymph from the central nodes and also receive lymphatic vessels accompanying the cephalic vein.
⭐
The apical nodes are therefore the final major axillary group before lymph leaves the axilla.
⭐ Very High-Yield Exam Point
”
🟢
Most lymph from the upper limb → humeral axillary nodes → central nodes → apical nodes
⭐
However, lymphatics associated with the cephalic vein can reach the apical nodes via deltopectoral/infraclavicular nodes.
9. Clinical Correlation — Venipuncture 🩸
🔻
Venipuncture is the puncture of a vein with a needle, usually to obtain a blood sample or establish intravenous access for administration of medications, fluids, or other substances.
🔻
Superficial veins are preferred because they are relatively large, superficial, visible or palpable, and accessible.
copy
The median cubital vein in the cubital fossa is the classic site for routine blood collection.
🔻
The cephalic and basilic veins, as well as veins arising from the dorsal venous network of the hand, may be used for intravenous cannulation and longer-term fluid administration, depending on the clinical situation.
🤔 Why Is the Dorsum of the Hand Important?
🔻
Veins on the dorsum of the hand are frequently used for peripheral intravenous access because they are superficial and readily accessible.
🔻
However, repeated cannulation can cause irritation or thrombophlebitis, so alternative sites may be required.
10. High-Yield Clinical Anatomy of Venipuncture
🔻
When performing venipuncture in the cubital fossa, the clinician must remember the relationship between the superficial veins and deeper structures.
✓
The median cubital vein lies superficially, while the bicipital aponeurosis lies deep to it. ✓
✓
The bicipital aponeurosis helps protect the brachial artery and median nerve, which lie deeper.
🔻
A needle inserted too deeply can potentially injure these structures.
🔻
The median cubital vein is therefore a preferred site, but anatomical variations must always be considered.
✓
The basilic vein should be approached with particular awareness of deeper structures because the basilic vein becomes associated with deeper neurovascular structures as it ascends the arm.
⭐ Axio-Appendicular Muscles of the Upper Limb
🔻
The axio-appendicular muscles connect the bones of the upper limb, particularly the pectoral girdle, with the axial skeleton.
🔻
They are important for positioning and moving the scapula and clavicle, thereby allowing efficient movement of the upper limb.
⭐
The anterior axio-appendicular group consists of four muscles:
🔻
Pectoralis major
🔻
Pectoralis minor
🔻
Subclavius, and
🔻
Serratus anterior.
⭐
These muscles are located on the anterior and lateral aspects of the thorax and primarily move or stabilize the pectoral girdle.
⭐ Pectoralis Major
🔻
The pectoralis major is a large, thick, fan-shaped muscle covering much of the anterior chest wall.
🔻
It is one of the most important muscles forming the anterior wall of the axilla.
🔻
Its lateral border forms the anterior axillary fold, which is an important surface landmark during physical examination.
🔻
The pectoralis major has two main parts:
✅
The clavicular head and
✅
The sternocostal head.
🟠 Origin
🔻
The clavicular head arises from the medial half of the clavicle.
🔻
The sternocostal head arises from the anterior surface of the sternum, the superior six costal cartilages, and the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle.
🔴 Insertion
🔻
The muscle inserts into the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus (intertubercular groove) of the humerus.
⬛
Intertubercular groove = Bicipital groove
✔️
A useful exam point is that the tendon of pectoralis major is twisted before insertion.
🟡
Fibers from the sternocostal part pass superiorly to insert more proximally, while clavicular fibers insert more distally.
🟪 Innervation
🟢
Pectoralis major is supplied by both the lateral pectoral nerve and medial pectoral nerve, mainly from the brachial plexus (C5–T1).
🎯
A common exam distinction is that both pectoral nerves supply pectoralis major, whereas pectoralis minor is primarily supplied by the medial pectoral nerve.
🟧 Actions
⭐
Pectoralis major is a powerful adductor and medial rotator of the arm.
🔻
The clavicular head flexes the arm, particularly from an extended position.
🔻
The sternocostal head can extend the arm from a flexed position.
⭐
When the upper limb is fixed, pectoralis major can help pull the trunk toward the upper limb. It can therefore contribute to movements such as climbing, pushing, and lifting the body.
🔻
It can also assist in forced inspiration when the upper limb is fixed, because it can elevate the thoracic cage.
⭐ Important Anatomical Relationships
✓
The lateral border of pectoralis major forms the anterior axillary fold.
✓
Between the pectoralis major and deltoid is the deltopectoral groove. The cephalic vein travels within this groove before entering the deltoid/pectoral (clavipectoral) triangle and eventually piercing the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein.
✓
The deltopectoral triangle is therefore clinically important for locating the cephalic vein and for venous access.
⭐ Clinical Importance
📝
The pectoralis major is commonly tested in relation to muscle tears, particularly during forceful activities such as weightlifting.
📌
Rupture may produce weakness of adduction and medial rotation of the arm and an abnormal contour of the anterior axillary fold.
🔻
The muscle is also important in breast surgery and reconstructive procedures because it lies directly deep to much of the breast.
⭐ Pectoralis Minor
🔻
The pectoralis minor is a small, thin, triangular muscle located deep to the pectoralis major.
🔻
It forms an important part of the anterior wall of the axilla.
🟠 Origin
🔻
Pectoralis minor arises from the anterior surfaces of ribs 3–5, near their costal cartilages.
🟪 Insertion
🔻
It inserts onto the medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula.
🟡 Innervation
🔻
It is primarily supplied by the medial pectoral nerve, usually from C8–T1.
🔻
The medial pectoral nerve typically pierces pectoralis minor before supplying it and may then continue to supply pectoralis major.
🟧 Actions
🔻
Pectoralis minor stabilizes the scapula against the thoracic wall by drawing the scapula anteriorly and inferiorly. 🟣🟣
⚪
It can also assist in protraction and downward rotation of the scapula.
🔻
When the scapula is fixed, pectoralis minor can elevate ribs 3–5 and therefore act as an accessory muscle of inspiration, particularly during forced breathing.
⭐ Important Clinical Relationship
🛡️
The pectoralis minor is an important landmark in the axilla because it divides the axillary artery into three parts.
⭐
This is an extremely high-yield anatomy point:
🔻
Axillary artery → divided into 3 parts by pectoralis minor.
🔻
The first part lies medial/proximal to pectoralis minor.
🔻
The second part lies posterior to pectoralis minor.
🔻
The third part lies lateral/distal to pectoralis minor.
✓
The branches of the axillary artery are therefore commonly remembered according to their relationship to pectoralis minor.
🔻
Another important point is that the medial and lateral pectoral nerves form the pectoral loop around the pectoralis minor region, making the muscle an important landmark for understanding the neurovascular anatomy of the axilla.
⭐ Subclavius
🔻
The subclavius is a small, cylindrical muscle located directly beneath the clavicle.
🔻
It extends from the first rib to the clavicle.
🟠 Origin
🔻
It originates from the junction of the first rib and its costal cartilage.
🔴 Insertion
🔻
It inserts into the subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle.
🟡 Innervation
🔻
It is supplied by the nerve to subclavius, derived mainly from C5–C6 of the brachial plexus.
🟧 Actions
🔻
Subclavius depresses and stabilizes the clavicle.
🔻
It also helps stabilize the sternoclavicular joint and can protect the underlying neurovascular structures by helping hold the clavicle in position.
🩺 High-Yield Clinical Point
✅
The subclavius can provide some protection to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus from forces transmitted through the clavicle.
⭐ Serratus Anterior
🔻
The serratus anterior is a broad, fan-shaped muscle covering the lateral aspect of the thorax.
🔻
Its characteristic saw-toothed digitations attach to the upper ribs.
🟠 Origin
🔻
It arises from the external surfaces of ribs 1–8, although some descriptions include the first 8 or 9 ribs depending on the anatomical classification used.
🔴 Insertion
🔻
It inserts along the anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula, with the inferior fibers extending to the inferior angle.
🟡 Innervation
🔸
Serratus anterior is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7).
⭐
This is one of the most important nerve–muscle associations in upper-limb anatomy:
⭐
Long thoracic nerve → Serratus anterior
🟧 Actions
🔻
Serratus anterior is the major muscle responsible for protraction of the scapula.
🔻
It also holds the scapula firmly against the thoracic wall.
⚪
Its lower fibers assist in upward rotation of the scapula, which is essential for raising the arm above the head.
⭐
Therefore, serratus anterior is especially important for overhead elevation of the upper limb.
🩺 Clinical Importance: Winged Scapula
🛡️
Damage to the long thoracic nerve causes paralysis or weakness of serratus anterior.
🌑
Because serratus anterior normally holds the scapula against the thoracic wall, its paralysis causes the medial border of the scapula to project posteriorly.
📝
This produces a characteristic winged scapula.
🔻
The condition becomes particularly obvious when the patient is asked to push against a wall.
🔻
A common cause is injury to the long thoracic nerve during trauma or surgical procedures in the axillary region.
📌 High-Yield Memory Point
📚
Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → protraction + upward rotation → injury causes winged scapula.
⭐ BREAST ANATOMY — HIGH-YIELD NOTES
1. Overview and Position of the Breast
🔻
The breast, or mammary gland, is a modified sweat gland specialized for the production and secretion of milk.
🔻
It is located in the superficial fascia of the anterior thoracic wall and does not possess a true complete capsule.
🔻
The breast lies mainly over the pectoralis major muscle (= hence called Breast muscle ), with its medial and lateral extent also related to the serratus anterior.
⭐
The posterior surface of the breast is separated from the deep pectoral fascia by loose connective tissue known as the retromammary space.
⭐
The retromammary space is clinically important because it allows the breast to move relatively freely over the underlying pectoral fascia.
🚫
Loss of this mobility may occur when a malignant tumor invades the deep fascia or surrounding structures.
copy
2nd to the 6th ribs
🔴 The breast usually extends vertically from approximately the 2nd to the 6th ribs and horizontally from the lateral border of the sternum toward the midaxillary line. Its exact dimensions vary considerably among individuals.
🔻
A lateral extension of breast tissue may pass through the lower part of the axillary region.
🔸
This extension is called the axillary tail of Spence. It is clinically important because breast pathology, including carcinoma, can occur in this region and may be encountered during examination of the axilla.
🟤
The overall size of the breast is determined largely by the amount of subcutaneous adipose tissue, rather than by the amount of glandular tissue.
✔️
Therefore, breast size does not directly indicate the amount of milk-producing tissue. 😎
2. Internal Structure of the Breast ⭐
⭐
The mammary gland is composed of glandular tissue, fibrous connective tissue, and adipose tissue.
🔻
The glandular component is organized into approximately 15–20 lobes, although descriptions commonly give a range of about 15–25 lobes.
🔻
These lobes are separated by connective tissue and fat.
🔻
Each lobe is further divided into smaller lobules, which contain the secretory units of the mammary gland.
⭐
The milk 🥛-producing units are the alveoli, also called acini.
🕯️
These are lined by secretory epithelial cells and surrounded by contractile myoepithelial cells.
⭐
During lactation, the alveolar epithelial cells produce milk, while contraction of the myoepithelial cells helps propel milk toward the ducts.
🔗 Suspensory Ligaments of Cooper
🔻
Fibrous connective tissue extends through the breast and forms the suspensory ligaments of Cooper.
🪣
These ligaments connect the dermis of the skin with the deeper fascial structures and support the breast.
🩺
Cooper's ligaments are clinically important in breast carcinoma.
📝
When a carcinoma infiltrates and shortens these fibrous structures, it can produce skin dimpling or retraction.
📝
This is an important examination point:
🔻
Breast carcinoma → infiltration of Cooper's ligaments → skin retraction/dimpling.
3. Lactiferous Duct System ⭐
🎯
The secretory alveoli drain into progressively larger ducts within the lobules and lobes.
🎯
These ultimately form the lactiferous ducts, which carry milk toward the nipple.
🎯
Each major duct approaches the nipple and opens separately onto the surface of the nipple.
🎯
Traditional anatomical descriptions describe a dilation of each lactiferous duct beneath the areola as a lactiferous sinus.
🎯
However, modern anatomical and histological studies indicate that the prominent milk-storage sinuses traditionally depicted in older textbooks are not as distinct as previously described. For examination purposes, the term lactiferous sinus may still be encountered.
🌑
The essential pathway to remember is:
Alveoli → small ducts → larger ducts → lactiferous ducts → nipple openings.
📌
During breastfeeding, milk is produced by the secretory alveoli and transported through the duct system toward the nipple.
4. Areola ⭐
🔻
The areola is the circular, pigmented area of skin surrounding the nipple.
🔻
It contains numerous modified sebaceous glands called areolar glands or glands of Montgomery.
🔻
These glands become more prominent during pregnancy and produce an oily secretion that helps lubricate and protect the nipple and areola during breastfeeding.
🔻
The color and size of the areola vary among individuals and may change considerably during pregnancy.
🔻
An important anatomical point is that the areola contains very little subcutaneous fat(= we can even say NO FAT) compared with the surrounding breast, and the nipple itself lacks adipose tissue.
🔻
The areola also contains smooth muscle and sensory nerve endings, contributing to the physiological response associated with nipple stimulation.
5. Nipple ⭐
🎯
The nipple is a conical or cylindrical projection located near the center of the areola.
👉
It contains the terminal openings of the lactiferous ducts.
🎯
The nipple contains abundant smooth muscle, particularly circular and longitudinal fibers.
🎯
Contraction of these muscles produces erection of the nipple in response to tactile stimulation, cold, or emotional stimuli.
🎯
The nipple itself is devoid of hair follicles and sweat glands and contains essentially no adipose tissue.
🎯
The nipple is classically located at approximately the level of the 4th intercostal space in males and nulliparous females, although its position is highly variable, particularly in females and with age, pregnancy, lactation, and breast size.
⭐ High-Yield Point
”
🔻
The nipple receives its principal sensory innervation from the 4th intercostal nerve. This is frequently tested.
6. Arterial Blood Supply of the Breast 🔴
⭐
The breast receives a rich arterial blood supply from branches arising mainly from the subclavian and axillary arterial systems, together with contributions from the posterior intercostal arteries.
⭐
The principal sources are the perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, especially those arising from the second to fourth intercostal spaces.
⭐
These vessels supply the medial portion of the breast.
⭐
The lateral thoracic artery, a branch of the axillary artery, supplies much of the lateral aspect of the breast.
⚡
The pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial trunk, also arising from the axillary artery, contributes to the arterial supply of the breast.
⭐
Additional blood reaches the breast through the posterior intercostal arteries, particularly in the second through fourth intercostal spaces.
🎯 Exam Summary
”
🌈
Remember the three major arterial sources:
⚡
Internal thoracic artery → medial breast
⚡
Lateral thoracic artery → lateral breast
⚡
Posterior intercostal arteries → posterior/lateral contributions
7. Venous Drainage 🔵
🔹
The venous drainage of the breast generally parallels its arterial supply.
🔹
Venous blood drains primarily toward the axillary vein, internal thoracic vein, and posterior intercostal veins.
🔹
The posterior intercostal veins are clinically important because they communicate with the vertebral venous plexus.
🔹
This provides a potential route through which malignant cells from breast carcinoma can reach the vertebral column.
🩸 Clinical Correlation
”
🔻
Breast carcinoma can metastasize to the vertebrae and other bones, and communication between the breast venous system and the valveless vertebral venous plexus is one anatomical pathway that can facilitate this spread.
8. Lymphatic Drainage of the Breast 🟢
🟢
The lymphatic drainage of the breast is extremely important clinically because breast carcinoma commonly spreads through lymphatic channels.
🟢
Most lymph from the breast drains toward the axillary lymph nodes.
🟢
Approximately 75% or more of breast lymph may ultimately drain to the axillary system, although the exact percentage varies among anatomical descriptions. The lymphatic vessels from the breast communicate with a subareolar lymphatic plexus, often called the plexus of Sappey.
🟢
Lymph from different regions of the breast then passes toward regional lymph nodes.
🟢
The major axillary lymph-node groups relevant to breast drainage include the pectoral (anterior), central, and apical nodes.
🔻
The pectoral/anterior axillary nodes receive much of the lymphatic drainage from the breast. From there, lymph may pass to the central nodes and subsequently to the apical nodes.
🔻
Lymph from the medial part of the breast can drain medially toward the parasternal lymph nodes, which are associated with the internal thoracic vessels.
🟢
Some lymphatic drainage may also pass inferiorly toward diaphragmatic, abdominal, or upper abdominal lymphatic pathways, although this represents a smaller component compared with axillary drainage.
🟢 Very High-Yield Clinical Point
🟢
Because breast lymph drains predominantly to the axillary nodes, examination of a patient with suspected breast carcinoma should include examination of the axillary lymph nodes.
9. Lymphatic Drainage and Breast Carcinoma
🟢
The lymphatic system provides an important route for the spread of breast carcinoma.
✅
A simplified pathway is:
🔻
Breast → pectoral/anterior axillary nodes → central axillary nodes → apical axillary nodes → supraclavicular region
🟢
Medial breast lymph may instead pass toward:
🔻
Breast → parasternal nodes → mediastinal lymphatic pathways
🟢
The axillary nodes therefore have major importance in staging breast cancer.
🟩
A sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node or group of nodes receiving lymphatic drainage from a primary tumor.
🔻
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is commonly used clinically to evaluate whether breast carcinoma has spread to regional lymph nodes.
10. Nerve Supply of the Breast
🔻
The breast receives sensory innervation primarily from the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 2nd–6th intercostal nerves.
🟡
The 4th intercostal nerve is particularly important because it provides the principal sensory supply to the nipple.
🔻
Autonomic fibers accompany the intercostal nerves and supply smooth muscle and blood vessels.
⭐
The breast does not receive its primary sensory supply from the brachial plexus; rather, its cutaneous sensation is mainly supplied by the intercostal nerves.
11. Clinical Quadrants of the Breast
🔻
For clinical examination and description of breast lesions, the breast is divided into four quadrants by horizontal and vertical lines crossing approximately through the nipple.
⭐
These are:
🔻
Upper lateral (upper outer) quadrant
🔻
Upper medial (upper inner) quadrant
🔻
Lower lateral (lower outer) quadrant
🔻
Lower medial (lower inner) quadrant
🚨
The upper lateral quadrant is clinically important because a large proportion of breast carcinomas occur there.
⭐
This is related in part to the relatively large amount of glandular tissue in the upper lateral region and its relationship with the axillary tail.
⭐
The breast should therefore always be examined systematically by quadrants, including the axillary tail.
12. Axillary Tail of Spence ⭐
🎯
The axillary tail of Spence is a superolateral extension of breast tissue that passes toward the axilla.
⭐
It is not a separate anatomical structure or an independent gland. Rather, it represents an extension of the breast tissue.
🎯
Its clinical importance is that breast disease, including carcinoma, may occur in this extension and may present as a mass in the axillary region.
⭐
Therefore, examination of the breast should always include the axillary tail and axillary region.
13. Important Clinical Changes
⭐ In Breast Carcinoma
Several classic physical findings of breast carcinoma can be explained directly by breast anatomy.
⭐
Skin dimpling or retraction occurs when a tumor infiltrates and contracts the suspensory ligaments of Cooper.
⭐
Nipple retraction may occur when a tumor involves or contracts the ducts and surrounding fibrous tissue beneath the nipple.
🟠
Peau d'orange, meaning an orange-peel appearance of the skin, occurs when lymphatic drainage of the skin is obstructed, producing edema around the hair follicles.
🟢
Axillary lymphadenopathy may occur because much of the breast's lymphatic drainage passes through the axillary lymph nodes.
🟣
Fixation of the breast to the chest wall may occur when a malignant tumor invades the underlying pectoral fascia or deeper structures, reducing the normal mobility provided by the retromammary space.
⭐ POSTERIOR AXIO-APPENDICULAR & SCAPULOHUMERAL MUSCLES
1. Classification of Posterior Axio-Appendicular Muscles
🔻
The posterior axio-appendicular muscles connect the pectoral girdle and upper limb to the axial skeleton.
🔻
They are divided into superficial and deep groups according to their position, while the scapulohumeral muscles connect the scapula directly to the humerus.
⭐
The superficial extrinsic muscles are the trapezius and latissimus dorsi.
⭐
They are mainly responsible for positioning the pectoral girdle and producing movements of the upper limb.
⭐
The deep extrinsic muscles are the levator scapulae, rhomboid minor, and rhomboid major.
✓
They primarily stabilize and move the scapula.
⭐
The scapulohumeral or intrinsic shoulder muscles 🔹 extend from the scapula or clavicle to the humerus.
🔻
They include the deltoid, teres major, supraspinatus 🔹, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. The last four constitute the rotator cuff.
✅
A useful distinction is that the axio-appendicular muscles mainly position the scapula, whereas the scapulohumeral muscles mainly act directly on the glenohumeral joint.
2. Trapezius ⭐
🔻
The trapezius is a large, triangular muscle occupying the posterior neck and upper back.
🔻
It provides an important muscular connection between the pectoral girdle and the axial skeleton.
🔻
Its fibers are arranged into three functional portions:
🎯
the descending (superior),
🎯
transverse (middle), and
🎯
ascending (inferior) parts.
⭐ Attachments
👉
The trapezius arises from the medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and spinous processes of C7–T12.
🎯
It inserts onto the lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula.
⭐⭐⭐ Innervation ⭐⭐⭐
🟡
The motor supply is from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
🔻
Sensory and proprioceptive fibers travel mainly through C3 and C4 spinal nerves.
🟧 Actions
🔻
The superior fibers elevate the scapula, while the middle fibers retract the scapula. The inferior fibers depress the scapula.
⭐
The superior and inferior fibers work together to rotate the scapula upward, allowing the glenoid cavity to face superiorly during elevation of the arm above the head.
🔺 High-Yield Point
🔻
The trapezius is one of the classic muscles tested for CN XI injury.
🔻
Damage to the spinal accessory nerve causes weakness of shoulder elevation and difficulty shrugging the shoulder.
🔻
The affected shoulder may appear depressed, and scapular movement can become abnormal.
🎯 Remember:
✅
Trapezius = Elevate + Retract + Depress + Upwardly rotate scapula
3. Latissimus Dorsi ⭐
🔻
The latissimus dorsi is a broad, flat, fan-shaped muscle covering much of the lower back.
🔻
It connects the trunk to the humerus and is particularly important during powerful movements such as climbing, swimming, rowing, and pulling the body upward.
🎯 Attachments
🔻
It originates from the spinous processes of approximately T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and inferior three or four ribs. Some descriptions also include the inferior angle of the scapula.
⭐
The muscle passes superolaterally and inserts into the floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
⭐⭐⭐ Innervation ⭐⭐⭐
🔻
It is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8).
🟧 Actions
🔻
Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
🟣
When the upper limb is fixed, it can pull the trunk upward. This is particularly important during climbing or performing a pull-up.
”
⭐ High-Yield Point
🟡
The thoracodorsal nerve should be remembered because it is clinically important during axillary lymph-node surgery, where injury can weaken latissimus dorsi.
📝
Latissimus dorsi = Extension + Adduction + Medial rotation
”
4. Levator Scapulae ⭐
🔻
The levator scapulae is a slender muscle located deep to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
🔻
It connects the upper cervical vertebrae to the superior medial border of the scapula.
🔻
It originates from the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4 and inserts along the medial border of the scapula superior to the spine.
⭐⭐⭐ Innervated ⭐⭐⭐
🔻
Mainly by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) with contributions from C3 and C4 cervical nerves.
🔻
Its principal action is elevation of the scapula. It also contributes to downward rotation of the scapula, causing the glenoid cavity to face more inferiorly.
🔻
When the scapula is fixed, bilateral contraction can assist extension of the neck, whereas unilateral contraction contributes to ipsilateral lateral flexion of the neck.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
Levator scapulae works together with the rhomboids and pectoralis minor in producing downward rotation of the scapula.
5. Rhomboid Minor and Rhomboid Major
⭐
The rhomboid muscles lie deep to the trapezius and connect the vertebral column with the medial border of the scapula.
🔻
They are important stabilizers of the scapula.
🔻 Rhomboid Minor
👉
Rhomboid minor arises from the lower ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 and T1.
👉
It inserts at the medial end of the spine of the scapula.
🔻 Rhomboid Major
👉
Rhomboid major arises from the spinous processes of T2–T5.
🎯
It inserts along the medial border of the scapula from approximately the level of the spine to the inferior angle.
⭐
Both muscles are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve, predominantly C5.
”
👉
Their major actions are retraction of the scapula, downward rotation of the scapula, and fixation of the scapula against the thoracic wall.
⭐ High-Yield Point ”
🎯
The rhomboids are particularly important for scapular retraction.
🔻
Rhomboids = Retract + Downward rotation + Stabilize
6. Scapulohumeral Muscles ⭐
⭐
The scapulohumeral muscles extend from the scapula or clavicle to the humerus and act directly on the glenohumeral joint.
⭐
The six major muscles are:
Deltoid, teres major, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis.
⭐
The last four form the rotator cuff, remembered as SITS:
”
🎯 S — Supraspinatus
🎯 I — Infraspinatus
🎯 T — Teres minor
🎯 S — Subscapularis
7. Deltoid ⭐
🔻
The deltoid is the large, thick muscle responsible for the rounded contour of the shoulder.
🟢
It has three functional parts:
🎯 anterior (clavicular),
🎯 middle (acromial), and
🎯 posterior (spinal).
👉
It originates from the lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula and inserts onto the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.
⭐
The muscle is innervated by the axillary nerve (C5–C6).
”
🟧 Actions
🔻
The anterior fibers flex and medially rotate the arm.
🔻
The middle fibers are the major abductors of the arm, particularly after the first approximately 15° of abduction.
🔻
The posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate the arm.
⭐ Important Concept: Initiation of Abduction ”
🔻
The deltoid does not initiate abduction.
🎯
The supraspinatus initiates the first approximately 15°, after which the deltoid becomes the major abductor.
Therefore:
⭐ 0–15° Abduction → Supraspinatus
⭐
15–90° Abduction→ Deltoid
Further elevation above 90° requires upward rotation of the scapula, principally through coordinated action of trapezius and serratus anterior.
🔻 Shunt Function
⭐
The deltoid contracts during abduction and helps prevent inferior displacement of the humeral head from the glenoid cavity.
👉
This stabilizing role is sometimes described as a shunt function.
⭐
High-Yield Clinical Point
💀
Injury to the axillary nerve, particularly with a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or anterior shoulder dislocation, can cause deltoid weakness or paralysis.
⭐
The patient may have difficulty abducting the arm beyond the initial range, and wasting of the deltoid produces a characteristic flattened shoulder contour.
8. Teres Major
⭐
Teres major is a thick, rounded muscle located inferior to teres minor.
🎯
It originates from the posterior surface of the inferior angle and adjacent lateral border of the scapula and inserts into the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
⭐
It is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve (C5–C6).
”
⭐
Its major actions are adduction and medial rotation of the arm, with some contribution to extension.
⭐ High-Yield Relationship
🚫
Teres major is not a rotator cuff muscle, despite its name and location near the rotator cuff muscles.
✅
A useful distinction is:
✅
Teres minor = Rotator cuff
🚫
Teres major = NOT rotator cuff
9. Rotator Cuff ⭐
🔻
The rotator cuff consists of four muscles:
⭐
Supraspinatus,
⭐
infraspinatus,
⭐
teres minor, and
⭐
subscapularis.
✓
Together, their tendons blend with the capsule of the glenohumeral joint and form a musculotendinous cuff around most of the joint.
🔻
The rotator cuff is extremely important for dynamic stabilization of the glenohumeral joint.
⭐
The glenoid cavity is relatively shallow compared with the large spherical head of the humerus. The rotator cuff muscles therefore continuously pull the humeral head toward the glenoid cavity and help keep it centered during movement.
🚫
Important Exception
👉
The rotator cuff reinforces the glenohumeral joint superiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly, but not inferiorly.
🔻
The inferior portion is therefore the relatively weak area of the joint capsule and is clinically important in shoulder dislocation.
10. Supraspinatus ⭐
👉
Supraspinatus occupies the supraspinous fossa of the scapula.
👉
It passes beneath the acromion and inserts onto the superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
⭐
It is supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5–C6).
⭐
Its major function is to initiate abduction of the arm during the first approximately 15° and to assist the deltoid thereafter.
❤️
It also contributes to stabilization of the humeral head.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
The supraspinatus tendon is the most commonly injured tendon of the rotator cuff.
⭐
Because it passes beneath the acromion, repetitive overhead activity can cause tendon irritation, degeneration, or tearing.
⭐
Supraspinatus = Initiates abduction
11. Infraspinatus ⭐
🔻
Infraspinatus occupies the infraspinous fossa of the scapula.
🔻
It inserts primarily onto the middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
⭐
It is supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5–C6).
⭐
Its principal action is lateral rotation of the arm, and it also stabilizes the humeral head within the glenoid cavity.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
Both supraspinatus and infraspinatus are supplied by the suprascapular nerve.
This is a frequently tested nerve–muscle relationship.
12. Teres Minor
🔻
Teres minor is a narrow muscle situated along the lateral border of the scapula.
🔻
It originates from the upper/middle portion of the lateral border of the scapula and inserts onto the inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
⭐
It is supplied by the axillary nerve (C5–C6).
🔻
Its principal action is lateral rotation of the arm. It also assists with adduction and stabilizes the humeral head.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
Teres minor is the only rotator cuff muscle supplied by the axillary nerve.
13. Subscapularis ⭐
🔻
Subscapularis is located on the anterior surface of the scapula and occupies the subscapular fossa.
🎯
It inserts onto the lesser tubercle of the humerus.
⭐
It is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5–C6).
”
⭐
Its principal actions are medial rotation and adduction of the arm, while also providing dynamic stabilization of the glenohumeral joint.
⭐ High-Yield Point
🔻
Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle located on the anterior surface of the scapula.
🔻
It is also the only SITS muscle inserting on the lesser tubercle.
⭐ Intermuscular Spaces of the Posterior Shoulder
🔻
Three clinically important spaces are found around the posterior shoulder:
📝
Quadrangular space, triangular space, and triangular interval.
🔻
They provide pathways through which important nerves and vessels pass between the axillary region and posterior shoulder/arm.
🔴 Quadrangular Space
⬛
The quadrangular space is bounded
🔹
Superiorly by teres minor, 🔹 Inferiorly by teres major,
🔹
Medially by the long head of triceps brachii, and
🔹
Laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus.
🟡
Its contents are the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.
🔻 Triangular Space
🔻
The triangular space is bounded
🔹
Superiorly by teres minor,
🔹
Inferiorly by teres major, and
🔹
laterally by the long head of triceps brachii.
🔴
It transmits the circumflex scapular artery.
🔻 Triangular Interval
🔻
The triangular interval is located inferior to the triangular space.
🔹
Its superior boundary is teres major
🔹
Its medial boundary is the long head of triceps brachii, and
🔹
Its lateral boundary is the shaft of the humerus/lateral head of triceps.
🟡
It transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery. 🔴
⭐
The radial nerve then travels with the profunda brachii artery in the radial groove of the humerus.
🔻 Ultra-High-Yield Exam Points
✅
The trapezius is supplied motorically by CN XI, while C3–C4 contribute sensory/proprioceptive fibers.
✅
The latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve and extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
✅
The rhomboids are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and retract the scapula.
✅
The deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve and is the major abductor of the arm after the first approximately 15°.
✅
The supraspinatus initiates abduction.
✅
The SITS muscles form the rotator cuff.
✅
The rotator cuff stabilizes the glenohumeral joint but is weak inferiorly.
🚫
Teres major is not a rotator cuff muscle.
✅
Teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle.
✅
The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
🔻
The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor.
🔻
The subscapular nerves supply subscapularis.
🔻
The supraspinatus tendon is the most commonly injured rotator cuff tendon.
🔻
A surgical neck fracture can injure the axillary nerve.
🟥
The quadrangular space contains the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral arteryhumeral
🔻
Triangular space contains the circumflex scapular artery.
🔻
The triangular interval contains the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery.

#EXAM POINT
#Exam point
🔻
Which one of the following statements is FALSE about the scapula?
A. The most palpable lateral part of the scapula is the acromion process.
B. The suprascapular nerve passes deep to the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the suprascapular artery and vein pass superficial to it.
C. The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch, then travels around the lateral border of the scapular spine through the spinoglenoid notch.
D. The suprascapular nerve passes above the superior transverse scapular ligament at the suprascapular notch.
E. None of the above.
✅
Accurate Answer: D
🤔 Why?
🟡〰
Suprascapular nerve → UNDER the ligament
🔴〰
Suprascapular artery → OVER the ligament
🤹‍♀
Classic mnemonic:
"Army over Navy"
Artery = over
Nerve = under
🎨
At the spinoglenoid notch, the suprascapular nerve passes around the lateral border of the scapular spine to reach the infraspinous fossa.
# SUMMARY 1
⭐ Brachial Plexus — High-Yield Comprehensive Notes
⭐ Overview and Supraclavicular Branches
🔻
The brachial plexus is a network of nerves formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of spinal nerves C5–T1.
🔻
It provides the major motor and sensory innervation to the pectoral girdle and entire upper limb.
🔻
The plexus is arranged sequentially from proximal to distal as:
🔻
Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Terminal branches
A useful mnemonic is:
⭐
Ready To Drinks Cold Berz
✓
Roots
✓
Trunks
✓
Divisions
✓
Cords
✓
Branches
🎯
The clavicle is used as an important anatomical landmark dividing the brachial plexus into a supraclavicular part and an infraclavicular part.
✅
The roots and trunks are mainly located superior to the clavicle, whereas the divisions and cords are associated with the region around and inferior to the clavicle and axilla.
🎯
Supraclavicular branches
Four important branches arise before the plexus reaches the cords.
🎯
Two arise from the roots, while two arise from the superior trunk.
👉
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) arises from the C5 root and supplies the rhomboid major, rhomboid minor, and levator scapulae. It is important for scapular retraction and elevation.
🔻
Long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) arises from the roots and descends along the lateral thoracic wall to supply the serratus anterior. Injury causes winging of the scapula, particularly when the patient pushes against a wall.
🔻
Suprascapular nerve (C5–C6) arises from the superior trunk. It passes through the suprascapular notch deep to the superior transverse scapular ligament and supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus. It is involved in initiation of shoulder abduction and lateral rotation.
🔻
Nerve to subclavius (C5–C6) also arises from the superior trunk and supplies the subclavius muscle.
⭐ Roots, Trunks and Divisions
🔻
The roots of the brachial plexus are formed by the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1.
✓
These roots emerge from the intervertebral foramina and pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
🎯
They then descend toward the superior part of the thorax and clavicular region.
⭐
The five roots unite to form three trunks.
🔻
Superior trunk
👉
The C5 and C6 roots unite to form the superior trunk.
🔻
Middle trunk
👉
The C7 root continues directly as the middle trunk.
🔻
Inferior trunk
👉
The C8 and T1 roots unite to form the inferior trunk.
⭐ Therefore:
🔻
C5 + C6 → Superior trunk
🔻
C7 → Middle trunk
🔻
C8 + T1 → Inferior trunk
🎯
Each trunk subsequently divides into an anterior division and a posterior division. Thus, there are: 3 anterior divisions + 3 posterior divisions.
⭐
Functional significance of the divisions
👉
