The divisions are clinically and anatomically important because they reflect the general organization of the upper limb.
🔻
The anterior divisions mainly contribute to nerves supplying the flexor/anterior compartments of the limb.
🔻
The posterior divisions mainly contribute to nerves supplying the extensor/posterior compartments.
⭐
This is not an absolute rule for every muscle, but it is an extremely useful framework for understanding the plexus.
⭐
Relationship to major landmarks
🎯
The brachial plexus changes its anatomical relationship as it travels toward the upper limb.
📍
The roots and trunks are located mainly in the neck and supraclavicular region.
📍
The divisions are located posterior to the clavicle.
📍
The cords are located in the axilla and are named according to their relationship to the second part of the axillary artery. 🔴
⭐ Formation of the Cords
👉
Within the axilla, the six divisions reorganize to form three cords.
👉
Their names are based on their relationship to the axillary artery.
🔻
Lateral cord
👉
The lateral cord is formed by the union of the anterior divisions of the superior and middle trunks.Therefore:
Anterior division of superior trunk + anterior division of middle trunk → Lateral cord
🎯
The lateral cord ultimately contributes to the musculocutaneous nerve and the median nerve.
🔻
Medial cord
👉
The medial cord is the continuation of the anterior division of the inferior trunk.
✓
It gives rise to the ulnar nerve, the medial root of the median nerve, and several other branches.
🔻
Posterior cord
👉
The posterior cord is formed by the union of all three posterior divisions.Therefore:
Posterior divisions of superior + middle + inferior trunks → Posterior cord.
✓
The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves, as well as nerves supplying muscles of the posterior shoulder and axilla.
⭐ Essential exam concept
”
🧠
Remember:
👉
Lateral cord = anterior divisions of upper 2 trunks
👉
Medial cord = anterior division of inferior trunk
👉
Posterior cord = all 3 posterior divisions.
⭐ Branches of the Cords
🔵
Lateral cord
🔻
The lateral cord gives three important branches.
✓
The lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C7) supplies the pectoralis major and contributes to the pectoral nerve network.
✓
The musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7) pierces the coracobrachialis and supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis. It continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, providing sensation over the lateral forearm.
✓
The lateral cord also gives the lateral root of the median nerve.
🔵
Medial cord
🔻
The medial cord gives rise to five major branches.
✓
The medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1) supplies the pectoralis minor and pectoralis major.
✓
The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (C8–T1) provides sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the arm.
✓
The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C8–T1) provides sensory innervation to the medial forearm.
✓
The medial root of the median nerve joins the lateral root to form the median nerve.
✓
The ulnar nerve (C8–T1) is the major terminal branch of the medial cord and supplies many muscles of the forearm and hand.
🔵
Posterior cord
🔻
The posterior cord gives five important branches.
✓
The upper subscapular nerve (C5–C6) supplies the subscapularis.
✓
The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) supplies the latissimus dorsi, an important muscle for extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm.
✓
The lower subscapular nerve (C5–C6) supplies the subscapularis and teres major.
✓
The axillary nerve (C5–C6) passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. It supplies the deltoid and teres minor and provides sensation over the characteristic regimental badge area.
✓
The radial nerve (C5–T1) is the largest branch of the posterior cord. It supplies the muscles of the posterior arm and forearm and provides cutaneous sensation to portions of the posterior and lateral upper limb.
⭐ Important clinical concept
”
🔻
The median nerve is formed by contributions from both the lateral and medial cords.
⭐
Therefore: Lateral root + medial root → Median nerve
🔻
This is one of the most frequently tested relationships in brachial plexus anatomy.
💀 Brachial Plexus Injuries
💀 Erb-Duchenne Palsy
🔻
Erb palsy results from injury to the upper part of the brachial plexus, classically involving C5–C6.
🔻
The classic mechanism is excessive separation of the neck and shoulder, such as during a difficult birth or traumatic traction injury.
👉
The affected limb assumes the classic “waiter's tip” position.
👉
The arm is typically:
Adducted + medially rotated
👉
The elbow is:
Extended
👉
The forearm is typically:
Pronated
👉
The wrist may also be flexed.
⭐
High-yield association
🔻
Erb palsy → C5–C6 🚫 → Waiter's tip
🚨
A common nerve association is injury involving the axillary and musculocutaneous distributions, although the lesion is at the plexus/root level rather than necessarily a single peripheral nerve.
💀 Klumpke Palsy
🔻
Klumpke palsy results from injury to the lower brachial plexus, classically involving C8–T1.
🔻
It commonly results from excessive traction on an abducted upper limb.
🎯
Because C8–T1 contributions are important for the intrinsic muscles of the hand, the patient may develop a claw hand deformity.
⭐
The intrinsic hand muscles become paralyzed, producing:
Hyperextension at the MCP joints + flexion at the IP joints
🩺 Associated clinical finding
🛡️
If the T1 sympathetic fibers are also affected, the patient may develop Horner syndrome, characterized by:
Ptosis + miosis ± anhidrosis
📌 Therefore:
🧊
Erb = C5–C6 = upper plexus = waiter's tip
🧊
Klumpke = C8–T1 = lower plexus = claw hand ± Horner syndrome
🧊
Erb = C5–C6 = upper plexus = waiter's tip
🧊
Klumpke = C8–T1 = lower plexus = claw hand ± Horner syndrome
⭐ ARM & CUBITAL FOSSA — HIGH-YIELD ANATOMY NOTES
💪 Arm Cross-Sectional Anatomy
🔻
The arm is enclosed by the deep brachial fascia, which attaches to the humerus and sends medial and lateral intermuscular septa toward the humerus.
🔻
These septa divide the arm into two major osteofascial compartments:
🔻
An anterior compartment, primarily responsible for flexion, and
🔻
A posterior compartment, primarily responsible for extension.
🔻
The anterior compartment contains the three muscles of the arm: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis.
🟡 🔴 〰
The major neurovascular structures include the musculocutaneous nerve, median nerve, brachial artery, and basilic vein. The ulnar nerve also traverses the medial aspect of the arm but does not supply the muscles of the anterior compartment.
⬇️
It descends medially and passes posterior to the medial epicondyle at the elbow.
🔵
The cephalic vein remains superficial, traveling in the subcutaneous tissue along the lateral side of the arm.
⚪
The posterior compartment contains the triceps brachii and anconeus, together with the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels. The humerus forms the bony axis of the compartment.
⭐ High-yield point
⚡
The musculocutaneous nerve is the principal motor nerve of the anterior compartment, whereas the radial nerve supplies the posterior compartment.
✨
The ulnar nerve passes through the arm but does not innervate an arm muscle.
🟥 Brachialis
🔻
The brachialis lies deep to the biceps brachii and forms much of the floor of the anterior arm near the elbow.
🦴
It originates from approximately the distal half of the anterior surface of the humerus and inserts onto the ulnar tuberosity and coronoid process of the ulna.
🚫
Unlike the biceps, the brachialis inserts on the ulna. Therefore, its action is not affected by the position of forearm rotation.
💥
The brachialis is the primary flexor of the elbow and flexes the forearm whether the forearm is pronated, supinated, or in an intermediate position.
〰 🟡
It is supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6). A small lateral portion may receive innervation from the radial nerve, an important anatomical variation often mentioned in detailed anatomy.
⭐ High-yield point
✓
Biceps = powerful supinator + elbow flexor.
✓
Brachialis = primary elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.
🟥 Coracobrachialis
🔻
The coracobrachialis is a slender muscle in the proximal medial part of the anterior arm.
🔻
It originates from the tip of the coracoid process, together with the short head of the biceps, and inserts into the middle third of the medial surface of the humerus.
✔️
Its major actions are flexion and adduction of the arm at the shoulder. It also contributes to stabilization of the shoulder.
🔻
A particularly important anatomical feature is that the musculocutaneous nerve pierces the coracobrachialis after entering the arm. This is one of the most frequently tested relationships of the muscle.
🔻
The nutrient artery of the humerus commonly enters the bone near the attachment of coracobrachialis, making this region an important anatomical landmark.
🟥 Triceps Brachii
🔻
The triceps brachii is the principal muscle of the posterior compartment of the arm and has three heads: long, lateral, and medial.
∞
The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.
∞
The lateral head originates from the posterior surface of the humerus superior to the radial groove, whereas the medial head originates from the posterior humerus inferior to the radial groove.
🔻
All three heads converge into a common tendon that inserts primarily onto the olecranon of the ulna and blends with the fascia of the forearm.
🟡 〰
The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.
📝
Its major function is extension of the forearm at the elbow. The long head also crosses the shoulder joint and contributes to extension and adduction of the arm as well as stabilization of the shoulder.
📝
High-yield radial nerve relationship
⭐
The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery travel together in the radial groove on the posterior humerus, between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps.
🟥 Triceps Brachii
🔻
The triceps brachii is the principal muscle of the posterior compartment of the arm and has three heads: long, lateral, and medial.
∞
The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.
∞
The lateral head originates from the posterior surface of the humerus superior to the radial groove, whereas the medial head originates from the posterior humerus inferior to the radial groove.
🔻
All three heads converge into a common tendon that inserts primarily onto the olecranon of the ulna and blends with the fascia of the forearm.
🟡 〰
The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.
📝
Its major function is extension of the forearm at the elbow. The long head also crosses the shoulder joint and contributes to extension and adduction of the arm as well as stabilization of the shoulder.
📝
High-yield radial nerve relationship
⭐
The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery travel together in the radial groove on the posterior humerus, between the lateral and medial heads of the triceps.
🟥 Anconeus
🔺
The anconeus is a small triangular muscle located on the posterolateral aspect of the elbow.
☑️
It originates from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus and inserts onto the lateral olecranon and proximal posterior surface of the ulna.
🟡
It is supplied by the radial nerve and assists the triceps in extension of the forearm.
☑️
The anconeus also contributes to stabilization of the elbow joint and helps maintain appropriate tension in the joint capsule during movement.
✔️
Anconeus = assists elbow extension + stabilizes joint capsule.
🟧 Cubital Fossa
↘ Boundaries of the Cubital Fossa
🔺
The cubital fossa is a triangular depression located on the anterior aspect of the elbow.
⬆️
Its superior boundary is an imaginary line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus.
⬅️
Its medial boundary is formed by the pronator teres.
➡️
Its lateral boundary is formed by the brachioradialis.
⬇️
The floor is formed mainly by the brachialis medially and supinator laterally.
🔺
The roof consists of skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, and the bicipital aponeurosis.
🔺
The bicipital aponeurosis is particularly important because it passes medially from the biceps tendon and provides protection over deeper neurovascular structures.
🔺
Contents and Relations of the Cubital Fossa
🔻
The deep structures of the cubital fossa are classically remembered from medial to lateral as:
📝
Median nerve → Brachial artery → Biceps tendon → Radial nerve
🟡
Median nerve
🟡
Radial nerve
🔴
Brachial artery
⚪
Biceps tendon
🔺
The brachial artery lies between the median nerve and biceps tendon and terminates near the level of the elbow by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries.
🔻
The median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery and continues into the forearm between the heads of pronator teres.
🔻
The biceps brachii tendon lies lateral to the brachial artery and attaches to the radial tuberosity.
🟡
The radial nerve lies on the lateral side of the cubital fossa, deep to the brachioradialis region.
↘
It divides into the superficial branch of the radial nerve and the deep branch of the radial nerve, with the deep branch passing through the supinator.
🔺
The median cubital vein is located superficially in the roof of the cubital fossa. It commonly connects the cephalic vein laterally with the basilic vein medially.
🔺
The superficial region may also contain the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm, which provide cutaneous sensation to the forearm.
⭐ Important correction
🖐️
The accompanying deep veins of the brachial artery are venae comitantes and are present around the artery, but when asked for the major contents of the cubital fossa, the classic exam answer is:
👨‍⚕️
Median nerve → brachial artery → biceps tendon → radial nerve.
🔻
Forearm Compartment Overview
🟢
Anterior Compartment:
⭐
Contains flexor-pronator muscles, which are supplied mainly by the 🟡 median nerve.
🔵
Posterior Compartment:
⭐
Contains extensor-supinator muscles, which are innervated by the radial nerve 🟡.
💪
Anterior Compartment of the Forearm (Superficial Layer)
🧑‍🏫
Arrangement:
🔺
The anterior compartment muscles are organized into three layers (superficial, intermediate, and deep).
🔗
Superficial Layer
⚪
Common Origin: Attached proximally via a common flexor tendon on the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
💪
Superficial Muscles:
🔸
Pronator Teres:
↗️
Inserts onto the middle of the lateral surface of the radius; functions as a pronator and flexor of the forearm (innervated by the median nerve).
🔸
Flexor Carpi Radialis:
↗️
Inserts onto the bases of the 2nd metacarpal; flexes and abducts the hand at the wrist (innervated by the median nerve).
🔸
Palmaris Longus:
↗️
Inserts into the distal half of the flexor retinaculum; flexes the hand (innervated by the median nerve).
🔸
Flexor Carpi Ulnaris:
↗️
Inserts into the pisiform, hook of hamate, and 5th metacarpal; flexes and adducts the hand; innervated specifically by the ulnar nerve.
💪
Anterior Compartment (Intermediate Layer)
🔹
Flexor Digitorum Superficialis:
✂️
Origin & Course: Arises from the common flexor origin and passes down the forearm.
✂️
Insertion: Base of the middle phalanges of the medial four fingers (digits 2–5).
✂️
Innervation: Median nerve.
✂️
Action: Primary flexor of the middle phalanges at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints.
💪
Anterior Compartment (Deep Layer)
🔹
Flexor Digitorum Profundus:
✂️
Origin: Proximal three-quarters of the ulna and the interosseous membrane.
✂️
Insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of the medial four digits.
✂️
Innervation: Dual innervation by the ulnar nerve (medial portion) and median nerve (lateral portion). 🟡
✂️
Action: Flexes the distal phalanges at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.
🔹
Flexor Pollicis Longus:
✂️
Origin: Anterior surface of the radius and adjacent interosseous membrane.
✂️
Insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb.
✂️
Innervation: Median nerve. 🟡
✂️
Action: Flexes the thumb.
🔹
Pronator Quadratus:
✂️
Origin & Insertion: Extends from the distal quarter of the anterior surface of the ulna to the distal quarter of the anterior surface of the radius.
✂️
Innervation: Median nerve.
✂️
Action: Pronates the forearm.
🟠
Posterior Compartment (Superficial Extensors)
⚡
Innervation Rule: All muscles in the posterior compartment are innervated by the radial nerve.
🔗
Superficial Group Common Origin:
⚪
Attached proximally to the lateral epicondyle via a common extensor tendon.
💪
Superficial Layer Muscle Details:
🔸
Brachioradialis: Originates from the supraepicondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts onto the lateral surface of the distal radius (proximal to the styloid process); functionally acts as an elbow flexor.
🔸
Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus & Brevis: Originate from the lateral supraepicondylar ridge and lateral epicondyle; insert onto the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals; extend and abduct the hand at the wrist joint.
🔸
Extensor Digitorum & Extensor Digiti Minimi: Pass to the extensor expansions of the fingers; extend the digits at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.
🔸
Extensor Carpi Ulnaris: Originates from the common extensor origin; inserts into the 5th metacarpal; extends and adducts the hand at the wrist.
🔵
Posterior Compartment (Deep Extensors)
🔹
Supinator: Extends from the common origin and ulna to the proximal third of the radius; acts to supinate the forearm.
👍
Outcropping Muscles of the Thumb:
🔸
Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL), Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB), and Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) originate from the posterior surfaces of the radius and ulna and insert onto the thumb phalanges/metacarpal.
🔸
Action: Extend and abduct the thumb.
📖 Structures Passing Deep to Retinaculum (Inside Carpal Tunnel):
🟡
Median nerve.
🟡
Tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus.
⬆️
Structures Passing Superficial to Retinaculum: Tendon of palmaris longus, ulnar vessels, ulnar nerve, and palmar cutaneous nerve branches.
⚠️
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Compression reducing space within the tunnel; primarily affects the median nerve, causing progressive loss of motor coordination and thumb strength.
🖐️ Intrinsic Muscles of the Hand (Thenar & Hypothenar)
🧩
Compartmental Organization: Intrinsic hand muscles are grouped into five compartments (thenar, hypothenar, adductor, central, interosseous).
👍 Thenar Compartment:
🔸
Muscles: Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis.
🔸
Innervation: Recurrent branch of the median nerve.
🔸
Action: Oppose, abduct, and flex the thumb.
🔷 Adductor Compartment:
🔹
Muscle: Adductor pollicis.
🔹
Innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
🔹
Action: Adducts the thumb.
🤙 Hypothenar Compartment:
🔸
Muscles: Abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis, and opponens digiti minimi.
🔸
Innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
🔸
Action: Abduct, flex, and oppose the 5th digit (little finger).
🩻 Lumbricals and Interossei
🔷 Lumbrical Muscles (1st to 4th):
✂️
Attachments: Arise from flexor tendons and insert into the extensor expansions of digits 2–5.
✂️
Innervation: 1st & 2nd by median nerve; 3rd & 4th by deep branch of ulnar nerve.
✂️
Action: Flex metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extend interphalangeal (IP) joints of digits 2–5.
🔷 Dorsal Interossei (4 muscles):
✂️
Innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
✂️
Action: Abduct digits 2–4 from the axial line (“DAB”).
🔷 Palmar Interossei (3 muscles):
✂️
Innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
✂️
Action: Adduct digits 2, 4, and 5 toward the axial line (“PAD”).
✋ Cutaneous and Motor Innervation of the Hand
🟡 Median Nerve:
➡️
Enters via the carpal tunnel.
💪
Motor: Thenar muscles and 1st & 2nd lumbricals.
🖐️
Sensory: Lateral palmar surface, palmar aspects of digits 1–3 and lateral half of digit 4, and dorsal tips/distal halves of digits 1–3 and lateral half of digit 4.
🟢 Ulnar Nerve:
➡️
Enters anterior to flexor retinaculum via the ulnar canal (Guyon canal).
🖐️
Palmar & Dorsal Cutaneous Branches: Supply medial side of palm and medial half of dorsum of hand (digit 5 and medial half of digit 4).
🖐️
Superficial Branch: Sensory to palmar side of medial 1.5 digits.
💪
Deep Branch: Motor to hypothenar muscles, medial 2 lumbricals, adductor pollicis, and all interossei.
🔵 Radial Nerve:
💪
Motor: Supplies no intrinsic hand muscles.
👉
Extensor Indicis: Originates from the distal third of the ulna and inserts into the extensor expansion of the 2nd digit (index finger); extends the index finger into the “pointing position”.
🖐️
Sensory: Supplies skin/fascia over the lateral 2/3 of the dorsum of the hand, thumb base, and proximal parts of digits 1–3 and lateral half of digit 4.
🩸 Arteries of the Upper Limb: 1. Brachial Artery
💧 Overview & Origin:
👉
The primary arterial supply to the arm. It is the direct continuation of the axillary artery, starting at the inferior border of the teres major muscle.
📍
Termination: Course terminates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius, where it bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries.
🔹 Branches:
1.
Unnamed Muscular Branches
2.
Humeral Nutrient Artery (enters the nutrient foramen of the humerus)
3.
Deep Artery of Arm (Profunda Brachii) (runs in radial groove with the radial nerve)
4.
Superior Ulnar Collateral Artery (accompanies ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle)
5.
Inferior Ulnar Collateral Artery
6.
Radial & Ulnar Arteries (terminal branches)
🔥 Important Exam Points
”
✂️
The brachial artery is palpable in the medial arm and cubital fossa.
✂️
The profunda brachii artery accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove.
✂️
The superior ulnar collateral artery accompanies the ulnar nerve posterior to the medial epicondyle.
✂️
The brachial artery is the artery used for blood-pressure measurement because the brachial pulse is auscultated in the cubital fossa.
🩸 2. Arteries of the Forearm
🔪 Ulnar Artery
💧
Ulnar Artery: Larger terminal branch of the brachial artery.
🔹 Branches:
↘
Anterior & Posterior Ulnar Recurrent Arteries (participate in elbow anastomosis).
↘
Common Interosseous Artery: Divides into:
🔹
Anterior Interosseous Artery (supplies deep anterior compartment).
🔹
Posterior Interosseous Artery (supplies posterior compartment).
🔹
Recurrent Interosseous Artery.
↘
Palmar Carpal Branch & Dorsal Carpal Branch.
🔥 Important Exam Point ⭐
✂️
The ulnar artery passes into the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon canal.
✂️
The ulnar artery 🔴 lies lateral to the ulnar nerve 🟡 within Guyon canal.
🤚 3. Arteries of the Hand & Palmar Arches
🩸 Ulnar Artery Course & Superficial Palmar Arch
📍
Entry: Enters the hand anterior to the flexor retinaculum between the pisiform and hook of hamate via the ulnar canal (Guyon canal), positioned lateral to the ulnar nerve.
🔀
Terminal Division: Divides into the Superficial Palmar Arch (main termination) and the Deep Palmar Branch.
🖐️ Superficial Palmar Arch:
✂️
Gives rise to 3 Common Palmar Digital arteries, which anastomose with palmar metacarpal arteries from the deep arch.
✂️
Each common digital artery divides into a pair of Proper Palmar Digital Arteries supplying adjacent sides of digits 2–4.
🔥 High-Yield Point
”
✂️
The superficial palmar arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery, with contribution from the superficial branch of the radial artery.
🔴 Radial Artery Course & Deep Palmar Arch
📍
Course: Curves dorsally around the scaphoid and trapezium along the floor of the anatomical snuffbox.
📍
Entry: Enters the palm by passing between the heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous muscle, then turns medially between the heads of adductor pollicis.
🖐️ Deep Palmar Arch:
•
Formed mainly by the radial artery anastomosing with the deep branch of the ulnar artery. Lies across metacarpal shafts just distal to their bases.
🔹 Branches:
✂️
Gives off 3 Palmar Metacarpal Arteries, the Princeps Pollicis Artery (to thumb), and the Radialis Indicis Artery (to index finger).
⭐ High-Yield Point 🎯
”
✂️
Superficial arch → mainly ulnar artery.
✂️
Deep arch → mainly radial artery.
🦴 1. Glenohumeral (Shoulder) Joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
👉
Ball and socket synovial joint, allowing multiaxial movement.
🔧 Articulation:
👉
Humeral head articulates with the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula; held in socket by the musculotendinous rotator cuff muscles.
🔗 Joint Capsule:
👉
Attached medially to the glenoid cavity margin and laterally to the anatomical neck of the humerus.
🎯
Encloses the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii superiorly.
🎯
The inferior part is unreinforced by the rotator cuff and represents the weakest region.
🔗 Key Ligaments & Structures:
⭐
Glenohumeral Ligaments:
🔻
Strengthen the anterior capsule.
⭐
Coracohumeral Ligament:
🔻
Strengthens the capsule superiorly.
⭐
Coracoacromial Arch:
🔻
Formed by the coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament; overlies the humeral head to prevent superior displacement.
🔄 Movements:
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, and circumduction.
🩸 Vascular & Nerve Supply:
🔴
Blood Supply:
✓
Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries; suprascapular artery branches.
🟡
Innervation:
✓
Suprascapular, axillary, and lateral pectoral nerves.
🔥 Important Exam Points
”
✂️
The shoulder joint is the most mobile major joint and consequently is relatively unstable.
✂️
The glenoid labrum deepens the glenoid cavity.
✂️
The inferior portion of the capsule is the weakest, explaining the frequency of anteroinferior shoulder dislocation.
✂️
The long head of biceps brachii tendon is intracapsular but extrasynovial.
🦴 2. Elbow Joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
🚪
Hinge synovial joint.
🔧 Articulation:
👉
Trochlea and capitulum of humerus articulate with the trochlear notch of the ulna and head of the radius.
🔗 Capsule & Ligaments:
🖐️
Weak anteriorly/posteriorly; stabilized laterally and medially by collateral ligaments:
🛡️ Radial Collateral Ligament:
✅
Extends from lateral epicondyle and blends distally with the annular ligament of the radius.
🛡️ Ulnar Collateral Ligament:
✅
Extends from medial epicondyle to the coronoid process and olecranon of the ulna.
⚙️ Movements:
🔻
Flexion and extension.
🧠 Innervation & Blood Supply:
🟡
Musculocutaneous, radial, and ulnar nerves; arterial anastomosis around the elbow. 🔴
🔥 Important Exam Points
”
✂️
The elbow complex includes the humeroulnar, humeroradial, and proximal radioulnar joints.
✂️
The carrying angle is formed between the arm and forearm when the elbow is extended and supinated.
✂️
The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle, making it vulnerable to injury.
✂️
Supracondylar fractures of the humerus can injure the brachial artery and median nerve.
🦴 3. Proximal Radioulnar joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
🔺
Pivot synovial joint.
🔧 Articulation:
✅
Head of radius articulates with the radial notch of the ulna.
🔗 Key Ligament:
⭐
Annular Ligament attaches to the ulna anterior and posterior to the radial notch, creating a collar/ring that completely encircles the head of the radius.
⚙️ Movements:
💪
Pronation and Supination. 💪
🧠 Neurovascular Supply:
🔴
Supplied by radial portion of elbow anastomosis:
🟡
Innervated by musculocutaneous, median, and radial nerves.
⭐ Important Exam Point
”
✂️
The annular ligament holds the radial head against the radial notch while allowing it to rotate.
✂️
In young children, sudden traction on the upper limb can cause radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow").
🦴 3. Proximal Radioulnar joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
🔺
Pivot synovial joint.
🔧 Articulation:
✅
Head of radius articulates with the radial notch of the ulna.
🔗 Key Ligament:
⭐
Annular Ligament attaches to the ulna anterior and posterior to the radial notch, creating a collar/ring that completely encircles the head of the radius.
⚙️ Movements:
💪
Pronation and Supination. 💪
🧠 Neurovascular Supply:
🔴
Supplied by radial portion of elbow anastomosis:
🟡
Innervated by musculocutaneous, median, and radial nerves.
⭐ Important Exam Point
”
✂️
The annular ligament holds the radial head against the radial notch while allowing it to rotate.
✂️
In young children, sudden traction on the upper limb can cause radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow").
🦴 4. Distal Radioulnar Joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
🔺
Pivot synovial joint.
🔧 Articulation:
🟣
Rounded head of ulna articulates with the ulnar notch on the medial side of the distal radius.
🔗 Articular Disc:
⚪
A fibrocartilaginous disc binds the radius and ulna together and completely separates the distal radioulnar joint cavity from the wrist joint cavity.
⚙️ Movements:
👉
The distal end of the radius rotates around the head of the ulna during pronation/supination.
🧠 Neurovascular Supply:
🔴
Anterior and posterior interosseous arteries; anterior and posterior interosseous nerves. 🟡
🔥 Important Exam Point
”
✂️
During pronation and supination, the radius rotates around the relatively fixed ulna.
✂️
The fibrocartilaginous articular disc is part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).
🦴 5. Wrist (Radiocarpal) Joint
🔵 Joint Classification:
🔺
Condyloid synovial joint.
🔧 Articulation:
💿
Distal end of radius and its articular disc articulate with the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum — EXCLUDING ❌ the pisiform).
🔗 Ligaments:
🦀
Ulnar Collateral Ligament:
⭐
Styloid process of ulna to triquetrum.
🦀
Radial Collateral Ligament:
⭐
Styloid process of radius to scaphoid.
⚙️ Movements:
👉
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction.
🧠 Neurovascular Supply:
✓
Palmar and dorsal carpal arches; anterior interosseous nerve (median), posterior interosseous nerve (radial), and dorsal/deep ulnar nerve branches.
🔥 Important Exam Points
”
✂️
The pisiform does not participate in the radiocarpal joint because it articulates with the triquetrum separately.
✂️
The ulna does not directly articulate with the carpal bones.
✂️
Abduction of the wrist = radial deviation.
✂️
Adduction of the wrist = ulnar deviation.
#Summary2
🦴 The Pelvic Girdle (Pelvis)
❕
The pelvic girdle is a basin-shaped bony ring formed by:
🦴
Two hip (coxal) bones → anteriorly & laterally
🦴
Sacrum → posteriorly
🦴
Coccyx → posteriorly
🎯 Main functions
🔗
Connects the lower limb (appendicular skeleton) to the axial skeleton
🗿
Transmits the weight of the upper body → lower limbs
🛡️
Supports and protects pelvic organs
🦵
Provides attachment for muscles involved in posture and locomotion
❕ A. Components of the Hip (Coxal) Bone ”
Each hip bone develops from the fusion of three bones at the acetabulum:
1 Ilium 🦴
”
The ilium forms the superior and largest part of the hip bone.
🔹
Ala (Wing)
🪶 Expanded superior portion of the ilium.
Medially → forms the iliaca fossa
Laterally → contains the gluteal lines
🔹
Iliac Crest
The thick superior border of the ilium.
📍
It extends between:
🔹 ASIS = Anterior Superior Iliac Spine 🔹 PSIS = Posterior Superior Iliac Spine
🔹 Important landmarks
”
ASIS → anterior superior iliac spine
AIIS → anterior inferior iliac spine
PSIS → posterior superior iliac spine
PIIS → posterior inferior iliac spine
▼ Greater sciatic notch
❕
The greater sciatic notch is located inferior to the posterior inferior iliac spine and above the ischial spine.
2 Ischium 🦴
”
The ischium forms the posteroinferior part of the hip bone and contributes to the acetabulum.
🔹
Ischial Tuberosity
A large, roughened projection. Its importance:
🪑 Bears body weight when sitting 💪 Provides attachment/origin for the hamstring muscles
Ischial tuberosity = sitting bone 🪑
”
🔹
Ischial Spine 📍
A sharp projection that separates:
⬆️ Greater sciatic notch ⬇️ Lesser sciatic notch
3 Pubis 🦴
”
The pubis forms the anteromedial part of the hip bone.
It has 3 main parts:
🔹
Body
Forms the medial part of the pubis. Articulates with the opposite pubic bone at the pubic symphysis 🤝
🔹
Superior ramus
Extends laterally from the body. Contributes to the acetabulum.
🔹
Inferior ramus
Joins the ramus of the ischium. Together they form the:
🤝 Ischiopubic ramus
── Obturator Foramen
”
A large opening formed mainly by:
🦴 Pubis + Ischium
It is almost completely closed by the:
👉 Obturator membrane
💡 anatomical importance:
”
Structures pass through the small obturator canal located at the superior part of the obturator foramen.
🦴 Acetabulum 🥣
The acetabulum is a cup-shaped socket that receives the:
👉 Head of the femur
Together they form the:
🦴 Hip joint
The acetabulum is formed by all three parts of the hip bone:
Part Contribution ”
🦴 Ilium Superior
🦴 Ischium Posteroinferior
🦴 Pubis Anteromedial
▼
Acetabular Notch
There is an opening/notch at the inferior part of the acetabulum.
It is bridged by the:
👉 Transverse acetabular ligament
This converts the notch into a foramen, through which nutrient vessels pass to the hip joint region.
Acetabulum = socket 🥣
Femoral head = ball ⚾
→ Together = ball-and-socket hip joint.
”
⚖️ Male vs. Female Pelvis
Pelvic Feature Female Pelvis (Gynecoid) Male Pelvis (Android)
General Architecture Lighter, thinner, smoother, shallower Heavier, thicker, prominent markings, deeper
Pelvic Inlet Transversely oval / spacious Heart-shaped / restricted
Subpubic Angle / Arch Broad / obtuse (> 80° - 90°) Acute / narrow (< 70°)
Ischial Tuberosities Everted (turned outward, larger outlet) Inverted (turned inward, smaller outlet)
Sacrum Shorter, broader, less curved Longer, narrower, more curved
Obturator Foramen Oval or triangular Round
Acetabulum Smaller, faces more laterally Larger, faces more anteriorly
Male vs. Female Sexual Dimorphism
Because the female pelvis is adapted for childbearing, it exhibits distinct structural differences from the male pelvis:
🩺 Clinical Correlations
Pelvic Fractures:
”
Severe trauma (such as motor vehicle collisions) can fracture the pelvic ring, risking tearing of pelvic blood vessels (internal iliac branches), nerves (sacral plexus, obturator nerve), or visceral structures like the urinary bladder and urethra.
Pelvic Diaphragm Weakness:
”
Stretching or tearing of the levator ani and pelvic ligaments during childbirth or with advancing age can lead to uterine prolapse (The uterus can descend downward toward or through the vaginal opening)or urinary incontinence(The pelvic floor contributes to maintaining urinary continence.

If its support is weakened, involuntary leakage of urine can occur).
Hormonal Ligamentous Laxity:
”
During late pregnancy, increased levels of relaxin cause the interpubic fibrocartilage and sacroiliac ligaments to loosen, increasing pelvic diameters to facilitate delivery.
🦴 1. Bones of the Thigh
A. Femur 🦴
The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body. 💪
🔵 Head of Femur
The head forms about two-thirds of a sphere 🌕 and fits into the acetabulum of the hip bone.
🔹
Fovea capitis femoris
A small depression on the head of the femur.
It provides attachment for:
👉
Ligamentum teres capitis femoris 🔗
This ligament carries a nutrient branch of the obturator artery 🔺.
The artery in the ligament of the head of femur is particularly important in children for supplying part of the femoral head.
”
🔵 Neck of Femur
The neck connects the head ⚪ shaft.
📐
Angle of inclination
Normally approximately:
👉 125°
👨‍⚕️ Coxa Valga
”
Angle increases → >135°
🦴 Neck becomes more vertical/straight.
👨‍⚕️ Coxa Vara
Angle decreases → <120°
🦴 Neck becomes more horizontal.
🔵 Trochanters
⭐ Greater Trochanter
Large lateral projection on the proximal femur.
Provides attachment for several muscles:
👉 Gluteus medius
👉 Gluteus minimus
👉 Piriformis
👉 Obturator internus
😎 Greater trochanter = major muscle attachment site
⭐ Lesser Trochanter
A smaller posteroinferior projection at the base of the femoral neck.
It receives the insertion of:
👉
Iliopsoas tendon 💪
🔗 Intertrochanteric Structures
🔹
Intertrochanteric Line — ANTERIOR
A ridge between the greater and lesser trochanters.
It provides attachment for the:
👉
Iliofemoral ligament 🔗
🔹
Intertrochanteric Crest — POSTERIOR
A prominent ridge connecting the two trochanters.
😎 LINE = anterior ➡️
CREST = posterior ⬅️
”
🦴 Shaft of Femur
The posterior surface has the:
⭐ Linea aspera
A roughened longitudinal ridge running along the posterior femur.
It has:
🟢 Medial lip
🔵 Lateral lip
These provide attachment for several muscles.
⬆️
Proximally
The linea aspera continues toward the:
👉 Pectineal line
which provides attachment for:
👉 Pectineus
🦴 Distal Femur
The distal end has:
🔵 Medial condyle
🔵 Lateral condyle
These articulate with the tibia to form the knee joint. 🦵
⭐ Adductor tubercle
Located superior to the medial condyle.
Provides attachment for the:
👉
Adductor magnus tendon
🦴 B. Patella
The patella is the:
👉
⭐ Largest sesamoid bone in the body
It develops within the tendon of:
💪
Quadriceps femoris
🔹
Articulation
Posteriorly, the patella articulates with the:
👉
Patellar surface of the femur
⚠️ It does NOT articulate with the tibia.
”
🔹
Patellar ligament
The apex of the patella continues inferiorly as the:
👉
Patellar ligament
which attaches to the:
🦴
Tibial tuberosity
🎯
Functions of Patella
🛡️
1. Protection
Protects the quadriceps tendon/knee joint from mechanical stress.
⚙️
2. Increases leverage
Moves the quadriceps tendon farther away from the axis of the knee joint.
➕
This increases the mechanical advantage of quadriceps during knee extension. 💪
Bones of the Leg
🦴 A. Tibia
The tibia is the medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg.
🔹 Proximal End
The proximal tibia has:
✔️ Medial condyle
✔️ Lateral condyle
These articulate with the medial and lateral femoral condyles, forming the knee joint 🦵.
🔹 Tibial Tuberosity
A prominent projection on the anterior proximal tibia.
It receives the:
👉 Patellar ligament
🔹 Distal Tibia
The distal tibia forms the:
⭐ Medial malleolus
This forms the prominent medial part of the ankle.
It articulates with the Talus 🦴.
Posterior Grooves:
The posterior aspect provides grooves for the tendons of:
👉 Tibialis posterior
👉 Flexor digitorum longus
👉 Flexor hallucis longus
The medial malleolus also provides attachment for the Deltoid ligament 🔗.
🦴 B. Fibula
The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg. Its main roles are muscle attachment and ankle stabilization.
🔹 Head of Fibula
The fibular head articulates with the lateral condyle of the tibia, forming the superior tibiofibular joint.
It also provides attachment for:
🔗 Fibular collateral ligament
💪 Biceps femoris
⚠️ Fibular Neck
”
The common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds around the neck of the fibula.
Therefore:
🚨
Fibular neck fracture → common fibular nerve injury
👉 Weakness of dorsiflexion + eversion
👉 Foot drop 🦶 ⬇️
🔵 Lateral Malleolus
The distal fibula forms the Lateral malleolus.
It extends:
✔️ More inferiorly
✔️ More posteriorly
than the medial malleolus.
It articulates with the Talus.
🔗 Ligaments Attached:
🔹 Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
🔹 Posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL)
🔹 Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL)
🧠
These are the major lateral ankle ligaments.
Feature / Aspect Tibia (Medial) Fibula (Lateral)
Weight-Bearing Main weight-bearing bone of the leg Non-weight-bearing (muscle attachment only)
Proximal End Medial & lateral condyles, intercondylar eminence Head & apex (biceps femoris & FCL attachment)
Vulnerable Nerve N/A Common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around neck
Distal Projection Medial malleolus (shorter, anterior) Lateral malleolus (longer, extends more inferior/posterior)
Ankle Articulation Articulates directly with talus at ankle joint Articulates with talus laterally; stabilizes mortise
🦶 Bones of the Ankle & Foot
The foot contains 26 bones:
”
🦴 7 Tarsals
🦴 5 Metatarsals
🦴 14 Phalanges
🧠 7 + 5 + 14 = 26
🦴 A. Tarsal Bones — 7
1 Talus ⭐
The talus transmits body weight:
Tibia → Talus → Foot
⚠️ Unique feature:
👉 No muscle attaches to the talus.
”
Its head contributes to the medial longitudinal arch.
2 Calcaneus 🦶
The largest and strongest tarsal bone, forming the heel.
It receives the:
👉 Tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon) 💪
⭐ Sustentaculum tali
A shelf-like projection on the medial calcaneus.
It:
🦴 Supports the head of the talus
🦴 Provides a groove inferiorly for the flexor hallucis longus tendon
🧠 Sustentaculum = support
”
3 Navicular ⛵
Boat-shaped bone. Located between:
👉 Head of talus 🌕 three cuneiforms
4 Cuboid 🧊
The most lateral tarsal bone.
Its inferior surface has a groove for:
👉 Fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon
⭐ It is the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch.
5 Cuneiforms 🔺
There are 3 cuneiform bones:
🟢 Medial
🟡 Intermediate
🔵 Lateral
They are wedge-shaped.
B. Metatarsals & Phalanges
”
Metatarsals — 5
Numbered: I → V from: Medial → lateral
⭐ 1st metatarsal
Its head has two prominent sesamoid bones. 🦴🦴
These are associated with the great toe and help protect/take load from the tendon structures underneath the first metatarsal head.
Phalanges — 14
🦶 Great toe (hallux) has 2 phalanges: Proximal + distal
🦶 Toes II–V have 3 phalanges each: Proximal + middle + distal
🧠 Great toe = 2
🧠 Other toes = 3 each
”
🦴 C. Arches of the Foot
”
The arches allow the foot to:
🛡️ Absorb shock
⚖️ Distribute body weight
⛰️ Adapt to uneven surfaces
🦘 Act as a spring during walking
🦴 1. Medial Longitudinal Arch
Bones:
🦴 Calcaneus
🦴 Talus
🦴 Navicular
🦴 3 cuneiforms
🦴 3 medial metatarsals
⭐ Keystone: Head of talus
🔗 Important support:
👉 Spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament
👉 Flexor hallucis longus also contributes dynamically.
⚠️ Clinical
Collapse → Pes planus (flat foot) 🦶 ⬇️
🦴 2. Lateral Longitudinal Arch
Bones:
🦴 Calcaneus
🦴 Cuboid
🦴 4th & 5th metatarsals
⭐ Keystone: Cuboid
🔗 Support:
🔹 Long plantar ligament
🔹 Short plantar ligament
💪 Fibularis longus tendon
🦴 3. Transverse Arch
The transverse arch runs: Medial ↔ lateral
🔹 Proximal part
Formed by:
✔️ Cuneiforms
✔️ Cuboid
✔️ Bases of metatarsals
Supported importantly by:
👉 Fibularis longus tendon 💪
🔹 Distal part
Formed by: Heads of the metatarsals
Maintained by:
👉 Transverse head of adductor hallucis 💪
CLINICAL CORRELATIONS
1 Femoral Neck Fracture 🦴
A fracture of the femoral neck can interrupt the blood supply to the femoral head.
💧 Most important vessel:
👉 Medial circumflex femoral artery
⬇️
Reduced blood supply to femoral head
⬇️
⚠️ Avascular necrosis (AVN)
Femoral neck fracture → AVN of femoral head
”
especially because the important retinacular vessels can be disrupted.
2 Posterior Dislocation of Hip 🚗💥
Classic mechanism:
👉 Dashboard injury 💥
During a head-on collision, the knee strikes the dashboard while the hip is flexed.
The femoral head is driven:
➡️ Posteriorly
Clinical appearance:
The affected limb becomes:
⬇️ Shortened
➡️ Adducted
🔄 Medially rotated
🧠 Posterior hip dislocation = SAD
Shortened
Adducted
Internally rotated
”
⚠️ Major complication
👉 Sciatic nerve injury 🧠
3 ⚠️ Fracture of Fibular Neck
The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck.
Therefore:
🦴 Fibular neck fracture
⬇️
Common fibular nerve injury
⬇️
Dorsiflexion weakness
Eversion weakness
⬇️
👉 Foot drop 🦶⬇️
🦵 Characteristic gait:
👉 High-stepping gait
The patient lifts the knee excessively to prevent the toes from dragging on the ground.
4 💥 Pott's Fracture
Classically associated with:
👉 Forced eversion of the foot 🦶🚨
This can cause:
🦴 Fracture of distal fibula/lateral malleolus possibly
🔗 Rupture of deltoid ligament
or
🦴 Avulsion/fracture of the medial malleolus
⚠️
It represents an ankle fracture-dislocation pattern, rather than simply an isolated fibular fracture.
5 🥾 March Fracture
A stress/fatigue fracture of a metatarsal.
Commonly:
👉 2nd or 3rd metatarsal
Cause:
Repeated/prolonged loading:
🦵 Long-distance walking
🏃 Repetitive exercise
🥾 Prolonged marching
Hence the name: March fracture 🥾
6 🏃 Achilles Tendon Rupture
The Achilles tendon is the:
👉 Tendo calcaneus
It connects the gastrocnemius + soleus complex to the calcaneus.
Together these muscles form the major component of the:
👉 Triceps surae
If Achilles tendon ruptures:
✔️ Powerful plantar flexion is lost
✔️ Pushing off during walking/running becomes difficult
⭐
Classic clinical finding
Achilles rupture → weak plantar flexion + difficulty standing on tiptoes 🦶⬆️
🦵 Fascia Lata
The fascia lata is the strong, membranous deep fascia that invests the muscles of the thigh like a sleeve.
”
Proximally, it attaches to:
✔️ Pubic symphysis
✔️ Pubic crest
✔️ Pubic rami
✔️ Ischial tuberosity
✔️ Inguinal ligament
✔️ Sacrotuberous ligament
✔️ Sacrum and coccyx
Laterally, it becomes markedly thickened to form the iliotibial tract (IT tract). ➡️
”
The IT tract receives insertions from:
🔹 Gluteus maximus 🍑
🔹 Tensor fasciae latae
📏 Saphenous Opening (Saphenous Hiatus / Fossa Ovalis)
”
An oval opening in the upper anteromedial part of the fascia lata. Located just inferior to the medial end of the inguinal ligament. It is covered by a thin, sieve-like layer called the cribriform fascia.
📝 What passes through the saphenous opening?
The most important structure is:
🔴 Great saphenous vein → Femoral vein
It also transmits:
🔴 Superficial epigastric vessels
🔴 Superficial circumflex iliac vessels
🔴 Superficial external pudendal vessels
🦋 Superficial lymphatic vessels
The great saphenous vein passes through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein.
”
Why is fascia lata important?
🔄
It limits outward expansion of muscles.
When a muscle contracts, it becomes shorter and thicker. The fascia surrounding it resists excessive outward expansion. This helps the muscle generate useful force.
🔄
Helps venous return ⭐
When thigh muscles contract, they can compress veins within/among the muscles.
Muscle contraction
⬇️
Compression of veins
⬇️
Blood pushed toward heart
This contributes to the muscle pump that helps prevent blood from pooling in the lower limb.
Muscle contraction = squeezing veins = venous return ⬆️
This is particularly important when you're standing or walking.
”
Three intermuscular septa extend from the fascia lata toward the femur, particularly the linea aspera.
These septa divide the thigh into:
🔴 Anterior compartment
🟢 Medial compartment
🔵 Posterior compartment
Why divide the muscles into compartments?
Because each compartment generally contains muscles with related:
🔹 Actions
🔹 Nerve supply
🔹 Blood supply
🩸 Venous Drainage of the Lower Limb
The venous system has 3 main components:
🩸
1. Superficial veins
Located in the superficial fascia.
🩸
2. Deep veins
Located deep to the deep fascia and generally accompany arteries.
🔗
3. Perforating veins
Connect the superficial and deep systems.
⬆️ Overall pathway
Superficial veins ➡️ Perforating veins ➡️ Deep veins ➡️ Popliteal vein ➡️ Femoral vein ➡️ External iliac vein

⬆️ Blood is therefore returned toward the heart.
”
A. Superficial Veins
”
🦵 Great Saphenous Vein (GSV)
📍 Origin: Begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot.
⬆️ Course:
✔️ Passes anterior to the medial malleolus.
✔️ Ascends along the medial side of the leg.
✔️ Continues along the medial side of the knee and thigh.
✔️ Accompanied by the saphenous nerve 🧠.
📖 Termination:
✔️ Passes through the saphenous opening.
✔️ Pierces the cribriform fascia.
✔️ Joins the femoral vein.
Great Saphenous = Anterior to Medial Malleolus
👉 GSV → Femoral vein
”
🔴 Important tributaries near the saphenous opening:
Superficial epigastric vein
Superficial circumflex iliac vein
Superficial external pudendal vein
Lateral femoral cutaneous vein
Accessory saphenous vein
🦵 Small Saphenous Vein (SSV)
📍 Origin: Begins from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch.
⬆️ Course:
✔️ Passes posterior to the lateral malleolus.
✔️ Ascends along the posterior midline of the leg.
✔️ Accompanies the sural nerve 🧠.
📖 Termination:
✔️ Pierces the deep fascia in the popliteal fossa.
✔️ Usually drains into the popliteal vein.
✔️ Accompanies the sural nerve 🧠.
Small Saphenous = Posterior to Lateral Malleolus
👉 SSV → Popliteal vein
”
B. Deep Veins
”
Deep veins generally accompany the major arteries as venae comitantes.
🦴 Anterior tibial veins
🦴 Posterior tibial veins
🦴 Peroneal (fibular) veins
⬇️
These unite around the lower border of the popliteus muscle to form:
➡️ Popliteal vein
🦵 Popliteal vein
✔️ Ascends through the popliteal fossa.
✔️ Receives the small saphenous vein.
✔️ Passes through the adductor hiatus.
✔️ Becomes the:
➡️ Femoral vein
🦵 Femoral vein
✔️ Ascends through the thigh.
✔️ Passes deep to the inguinal ligament.
✔️ Continues as the:
➡️ External iliac vein
⭐ Anterior tibial + Posterior tibial + Peroneal veins
⬇️
Popliteal vein
⬇️
Femoral vein
⬇️
External iliac vein
”
🔗 C. Perforating Veins
”
Perforating veins connect:
Superficial veins 🩸 ⬌ Deep veins 🩸
🚦 Direction of blood flow
Normally, valves allow blood to flow:
Superficial → Deep ⬇️
but prevent:
Deep → Superficial 🚫
Musculovenous pump
When the leg muscles contract:
💪 Muscle contraction
⬇️
Compresses deep veins
⬇️
Pushes blood upward ⬆️
⬇️
Helps venous return ❤️
This is particularly important because blood has to travel against gravity from the lower limb.
🦠 Lymphatic Drainage of the Lower Limb
There are two important superficial lymphatic pathways:
1. 🟢 Medial lymphatic vessels
Follow the:
Great saphenous vein 🔴
⬇️
Drain into:
Superficial inguinal lymph nodes 🟢
2. 🔵 Lateral lymphatic vessels
Follow the:
Small saphenous vein 🔴
⬇️
Drain into:
Popliteal lymph nodes 🟢
⬇️
Deep lymphatic vessels
⬇️
Deep/superficial inguinal lymph nodes
🟢
Superficial Inguinal Lymph Nodes
”
Located in the subcutaneous tissue of the upper thigh, near the termination of the great saphenous vein.
They receive lymph from:
🦵 Superficial lower limb
🫃 Anterolateral abdominal wall below the umbilicus
🍑 Gluteal region
🍆 External genitalia
🪑 Lower anal canal
Their lymph ultimately drains toward the external iliac lymph nodes.
🩺 Clinical Correlations
❤️ 1. Great Saphenous Vein & CABG
The great saphenous vein can be harvested and used as a graft during:
➡️ Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) ❤️
Because venous valves normally allow blood to flow in one direction, the vein may be reversed before being used as an arterial graft so the valves don't obstruct blood flow. 🔻
🧠 2. Saphenous Nerve Injury
The saphenous nerve runs close to the great saphenous vein in the leg.
Therefore, procedures involving the GSV, such as:
✂️ Vein stripping
📄 Vein harvesting
can injure the nerve.
This can cause:
⚡ Pain
😬 Paresthesia
😴 Numbness
in the medial leg and medial foot.
🪢 3. Varicose Veins
Normally:
Superficial veins → Perforating veins → Deep veins ✅
Perforating veins contain valves that normally prevent:
Deep → Superficial 🚫
If these valves become incompetent:
🔵 High-pressure blood from deep veins
⬇️
🔗 Through incompetent perforators
⬇️
🟢 Superficial veins
⬇️
💥 Veins become dilated + elongated + tortuous
⬇️
🪢 Varicose veins
The great saphenous system is commonly involved.
🫄 4. Femoral Hernia & Saphenous Opening
A femoral hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through the:
Femoral ring → Femoral canal
⬇️
As the hernia enlarges, it may turn anteriorly and emerge through the:
➡️ Saphenous opening
📍
It presents as a mass in the upper anteromedial thigh, classically inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
🧠
Important distinction:
Femoral hernia = below and lateral to pubic tubercle 📍
This helps distinguish it from an inguinal hernia, which is generally above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
”
🔬 HISTOLOGY
🧬 Welcome to Histology
📌
Ready for your Histology notes. Start pasting your content below!
🦠 Histology of Integumentary System
🎯 1. General Overview & Functions of the Integumentary System
✨ A. Definition & Components
🔻
The integumentary system is the body's outer protective system and the most superficial of the 11 organ systems.
🔻
It consists of the cutaneous membrane (skin) and accessory structures.
🔻
Hairs provide protection, sensation, and limited temperature regulation.
🔻
Nails protect the ends of the fingers and toes.
🔻
Sebaceous glands produce sebum, which lubricates and helps protect the skin.
🔻
Eccrine glands produce sweat and are important in thermoregulation.
🔻
Apocrine glands produce specialized sweat secretions.
🔻
Mammary glands are specialized glands that produce milk.
🔻
Sensory receptors detect touch, pressure, pain, temperature, and other stimuli.
✔️
Integumentary system = Skin + hair + nails + glands + sensory receptors
✨ B. Size & Surface Area
🔻
The skin is the largest single organ of the human body.
🔻
It accounts for approximately 10–15% of total body weight.
🔻
In adults, it covers approximately 1.5–2 m² of body surface.
🔻
Because it covers the external surface, the skin forms a major interface between the internal environment and the outside world.
✨ C. Protection
🔻
The skin forms a physical barrier that protects deeper tissues from mechanical injury, chemicals, pathogens, and excessive water loss.
🔻
The outer layer helps resist abrasion and limits water movement through the skin.
🔻
Skin secretions and resident immune cells provide additional chemical and immune protection.
✔️
Protection = physical barrier + chemical defense + immune defense
✨ D. Sensory Reception
🔻
The skin contains many sensory receptors connected to the nervous system.
🔻
These receptors detect touch, pressure, pain, temperature, itching, and vibration.
🔻
Sensory information is transmitted through peripheral nerves toward the central nervous system (CNS).
✔️
Skin = major sensory interface with the external environment
✨ E. Thermoregulation
🔻
The integumentary system helps maintain a stable body temperature.
🔻
Sweat glands release sweat onto the skin surface, and evaporation helps remove heat.
🔻
Vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and promotes heat loss.
🔻
Vasoconstriction reduces superficial blood flow and helps conserve heat.
🔻
Subcutaneous fat provides insulation and reduces heat loss.
✔️
Thermoregulation = sweating + blood-flow changes + insulation
✨ F. Metabolic & Other Functions
🔻
The skin participates in vitamin D production following appropriate ultraviolet exposure.
🔻
Subcutaneous adipose tissue provides energy storage, insulation, and cushioning.
🔻
The skin also helps limit excessive water loss from the body.
🔻
Hair and sensory receptors contribute to protection and environmental awareness.
✨ G. Overall Importance
🔻
The integumentary system functions as a protective barrier, sensory interface, temperature regulator, immune defense surface, and metabolic organ.
✔️
Integumentary system = Protection + Sensation + Thermoregulation + Immune Defense + Metabolic Support
🎯 2. Basic Layered Architecture of the Skin
✨ A. Epidermis
🔻
The epidermis is the superficial layer of the skin and is made mainly of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
🔻
It is avascular, so nutrients reach its cells by diffusion from blood vessels in the dermis.
🔻
The epidermis rests on a basement membrane and forms the body's primary external protective barrier.
🔻
It contains keratinocytes and specialized cells involved in pigmentation, immune defense, and sensation.
✔️
Epidermis = superficial + avascular + protective epithelial layer
✨ B. Dermis
🔻
The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is a strong, flexible connective-tissue layer.
🔻
It is highly vascularized and contains blood vessels, nerves, sensory receptors, and many skin appendages.
🔻
The dermis has two regions: the papillary layer and the deeper reticular layer.
🔻
The papillary layer contains dermal papillae and contributes to the connection between the epidermis and dermis.
🔻
The reticular layer contains stronger connective tissue that provides much of the skin's strength and flexibility.
✔️
Dermis = vascular + supportive + sensory + appendage-containing layer
✨ C. Dermal–Epidermal Junction
🔻
The boundary between the epidermis and dermis is an irregular, interlocking interface.
🔻
Epidermal ridges (rete pegs) extend downward into the dermis.
🔻
Dermal papillae project upward toward the epidermis.
🔻
Their interlocking arrangement strengthens attachment between the two layers and increases the surface area for exchange.
✔️
Dermal–epidermal junction = strong mechanical connection between epidermis and dermis
✨ D. Subcutaneous Tissue
🔻
The hypodermis, also called subcutaneous tissue or superficial fascia, lies deep to the dermis.
🔻
It consists mainly of adipose tissue and loose areolar connective tissue.
🔻
It provides energy storage, thermal insulation, cushioning, and protection.
🔻
It also helps anchor the skin to underlying structures such as muscle.
✔️
Hypodermis = insulation + energy storage + cushioning + anchoring
✨ E. Overall Arrangement
🔻
Epidermis → Dermis → Hypodermis → Deep tissues
🔻
The epidermis provides the external protective barrier.
🔻
The dermis provides strength, blood supply, sensation, and houses many skin appendages.
🔻
The hypodermis provides insulation, cushioning, energy storage, and attachment.
✔️
Skin architecture = protective surface + supportive connective layer + subcutaneous foundation
🎯 3. Detailed Histology of the Epidermis
✨ A. Epidermal Cell Types
🔻
The epidermis is a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium containing four major cell types.
🔻
Keratinocytes: The most abundant cells. They produce keratin, which strengthens and protects the epidermis.
🔻
Melanocytes: Produce melanin, the pigment that contributes to skin color and helps protect cells from ultraviolet radiation.
🔻
Langerhans Cells: Specialized dendritic immune cells that participate in detecting and responding to foreign substances.
🔻
Merkel Cells: Specialized sensory cells associated with light-touch reception.
✔️
Four epidermal cells = Keratinocytes + Melanocytes + Langerhans cells + Merkel cells
✨ B. Epidermal Strata
🔻
The epidermis contains four layers in thin skin and five layers in thick skin.
🔻
From deepest → most superficial: Stratum basale → Stratum spinosum → Stratum granulosum → Stratum lucidum → Stratum corneum
✨ 1. Stratum Basale
🔻
The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer.
🔻
It consists mainly of a single layer of columnar or cuboidal cells resting on the basement membrane.
🔻
It contains stem cells and actively dividing keratinocytes, allowing continuous replacement of cells lost from the surface.
🔻
Melanocytes and Merkel cells are also located in this layer.
✔️
Stratum basale = deepest layer + cell division + regeneration
✨ 2. Stratum Spinosum
🔻
The stratum spinosum lies above the basal layer.
🔻
It contains several layers of polygonal keratinocytes.
🔻
Cells are connected by desmosomes, which provide strong cell-to-cell attachment.
🔻
Keratin intermediate filaments form bundles called tonofibrils, contributing to the mechanical strength of the epidermis.
✔️
Stratum spinosum = strong cell connections + keratin production
✨ 3. Stratum Granulosum
🔻
The stratum granulosum contains several layers of flattened keratinocytes.
🔻
These cells contain keratohyalin granules, which contribute to keratin formation and organization.
🔻
They also contain lamellar granules, which release lipids into the spaces between cells.
🔻
These lipids help create a water-resistant barrier.
✔️
Stratum granulosum = keratinization + water barrier formation
✨ 4. Stratum Lucidum
🔻
The stratum lucidum is a thin, translucent layer found only in thick skin.
🔻
Thick skin is found mainly on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.
🔻
It consists of flattened, dead keratinocytes that lack visible nuclei and organelles.
✔️
Stratum lucidum = clear layer found only in thick skin
✨ 5. Stratum Corneum
🔻
The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis.
🔻
It consists of many layers of flattened, dead, non-nucleated keratinized cells called corneocytes.
🔻
These cells are filled with keratin and surrounded by lipid-rich material.
🔻
The stratum corneum provides the major physical, chemical, and water-resistant barrier of the epidermis.
🔻
Cells are continuously shed from the surface and replaced by cells produced in the deeper layers.
✔️
Stratum corneum = outer protective barrier + keratinized dead cells
✨ C. Epidermal Layer Sequence
🔻
Deep → Superficial: Basale → Spinosum → Granulosum → Lucidum → Corneum
🔻
Remember: “Before Signing, Get Legal Counsel”
✔️
Thick skin = 5 layers
✔️
Thin skin = 4 layers because the stratum lucidum is absent
🎯 4. High-Yield Comparison: Thick Skin vs. Thin Skin
✨ A. Thick Skin (Glabrous Skin)
🔻
Location: Found mainly on the palms of the hands, soles of the feet, and palmar/plantar surfaces of the digits.
🔻
Epidermal thickness: Approximately 400–1400 µm (0.4–1.4 mm).
🔻
Number of layers: Contains 5 epidermal strata, including the stratum lucidum.
🔻
The stratum corneum is especially thick, providing strong protection against friction and mechanical stress.
🔻
The granular layer is also prominent, reflecting active keratinization.
🔻
Thick skin lacks hair follicles, arrector pili muscles, and sebaceous glands.
🔻
It has prominent epidermal ridges and dermal papillae, contributing to fingerprints and strong attachment between the epidermis and dermis.
✔️
Thick skin = 5 layers + stratum lucidum + no hair follicles + no sebaceous glands
✨ B. Thin Skin
🔻
Location: Covers most of the remaining body surface.
🔻
Epidermal thickness: Approximately 75–150 µm.
🔻
Number of layers: Usually contains 4 epidermal strata because the stratum lucidum is absent.
🔻
The stratum corneum is thinner than that of thick skin.
🔻
The granular layer is generally thin or less prominent.
🔻
Thin skin contains hair follicles, arrector pili muscles, and sebaceous glands.
🔻
Its epidermal ridges are generally less prominent, producing a smoother surface in many regions.
✔️
Thin skin = 4 layers + no stratum lucidum + hair + sebaceous glands
✨ C. High-Yield Comparison
🔻
Thick skin: Palms and soles → 5 layers → stratum lucidum present → no hair → no sebaceous glands → very thick stratum corneum.
🔻
Thin skin: Most of body → 4 layers → stratum lucidum absent → hair present → sebaceous glands present → thinner stratum corneum.
✨ D. Important Anatomical Note
🔻
The terms “thick skin” and “thin skin” refer specifically to the thickness of the epidermis, not necessarily the total thickness of the skin.
🔻
Total skin thickness depends greatly on the body region because the dermis varies in thickness.
🔻
For example, the skin of the back between the scapulae can be around 4 mm thick overall.
🔻
The scalp may have an overall skin thickness of approximately 1.5 mm.
✔️
Thick vs. thin = primarily epidermal thickness, not total skin thickness.
🎯 5. Skin Pigmentation & Determinants
✨ A. Overview
🔻
Skin color is influenced mainly by three pigments: Melanin + Carotenoids + Hemoglobin
🔻
The relative amount, distribution, and condition of these pigments contribute to the visible color of the skin.
✨ B. Melanin
🔻
Melanin is the main pigment responsible for much of the variation in human skin color.
🔻
It is the only major skin pigment synthesized directly in the skin.
🔻
Melanin is produced by specialized epidermal cells called melanocytes.
🔻
Melanin is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine, with the enzyme tyrosinase playing an important role in the pathway.
🔻
Melanin helps protect skin cells from ultraviolet (UV) radiation by absorbing and dissipating some of the energy from UV exposure.
✨ Skin Color Variation
🔻
People generally have similar numbers of melanocytes, but melanocytes can differ in their activity and in the amount and type of melanin produced.
🔻
Differences in skin color therefore depend largely on the amount, type, distribution, and persistence of melanin within the skin.
✨ Albinism
🔻
Albinism refers to inherited conditions involving reduced or absent melanin production.
🔻
Some forms result from mutations affecting tyrosinase or other proteins involved in melanin synthesis.
🔻
Reduced melanin production results in significantly lighter pigmentation of the skin, hair, and eyes.
✨ Freckles & Moles
🔻
Freckles are localized areas of increased pigmentation caused mainly by increased melanin production.
🔻
Moles (nevi) are localized collections of melanocytes and may appear as pigmented spots on the skin.
✔️
Melanin = major determinant of skin pigmentation + UV protection
✨ C. Carotenoids
🔻
Carotenoids are yellow-to-orange pigments obtained mainly through the diet.
🔻
Foods such as carrots, sweet potatoes, and other plant foods can provide carotenoids.
🔻
Carotenoids can accumulate in subcutaneous adipose tissue and in the stratum corneum, particularly when present in high amounts.
🔻
Increased carotenoid accumulation can contribute a yellowish or orange tint to the skin.
✔️
Carotenoids = dietary yellow-orange pigments stored in body tissues
✨ D. Hemoglobin
🔻
Hemoglobin is the oxygen-binding protein found inside red blood cells.
🔻
Hemoglobin itself is not produced by the skin, but blood flowing through dermal blood vessels contributes to visible skin coloration.
🔻
The amount of visible blood flow and the oxygenation state of hemoglobin can influence the pinkish or reddish appearance of lighter skin.
✔️
Hemoglobin = blood pigment contributing to reddish or pinkish skin tones
✨ E. Overall Summary
🔻
Melanin → produced by melanocytes → brown to black pigmentation → major role in skin color and UV protection.
🔻
Carotenoids → obtained from diet → yellow-orange pigmentation.
🔻
Hemoglobin → found in red blood cells → contributes to pinkish or reddish coloration through dermal blood vessels.
✔️
Skin color = combined effects of melanin + carotenoids + hemoglobin + blood flow
🎯 6. Histology of the Dermis & Vascularity
✨ A. Dermal Layers
🔻
The dermis is a connective-tissue layer located beneath the epidermis.
🔻
It is divided into two continuous regions: Papillary dermis → Reticular dermis
✨ 1. Papillary Dermis
🔻
The papillary dermis is the superficial portion of the dermis and makes up approximately the upper 1/5.
🔻
It consists mainly of loose (areolar) connective tissue.
🔻
It forms upward projections called dermal papillae, which interlock with the epidermal ridges.
🔻
This interlocking arrangement strengthens the attachment between the epidermis and dermis.
🔻
It contains numerous capillaries and sensory receptors, allowing it to support the epidermis and contribute to sensation.
✔️
Papillary dermis = loose connective tissue + dermal papillae + capillaries + sensory receptors
✨ 2. Reticular Dermis
🔻
The reticular dermis forms the deeper and larger portion of the dermis, approximately the lower 4/5.
🔻
It consists mainly of dense irregular connective tissue.
🔻
It contains interwoven bundles of collagen fibers and elastic fibers.
🔻
Collagen fibers provide tensile strength and help resist stretching.
🔻
Elastic fibers allow the skin to stretch and return toward its original shape.
🔻
The reticular dermis contains many important skin structures, including hair follicles, glands, nerves, and larger blood vessels.
✔️
Reticular dermis = dense connective tissue + collagen + elastic fibers + skin appendages
✨ B. Cutaneous Circulation
🔻
The dermis contains an extensive network of blood vessels that supplies the skin and its structures.
🔻
Two major vascular networks are important: Deep cutaneous vascular plexus & Superficial subpapillary vascular plexus
🔻
The superficial vascular network supplies the upper dermis and contributes to the exchange of nutrients and gases.
🔻
Blood vessels also play an important role in temperature regulation.
✨ C. Thermoregulation
🔻
In cold conditions, dermal blood vessels undergo vasoconstriction.
🔻
Vasoconstriction decreases blood flow near the skin surface and helps reduce heat loss.
🔻
In warm conditions, dermal blood vessels undergo vasodilation.
🔻
Vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface, allowing more heat to be transferred to the environment.
✔️
Cold → Vasoconstriction → Heat conservation
✔️
Warm → Vasodilation → Heat dissipation
✨ D. Overall Summary
🔻
Papillary dermis → loose connective tissue → dermal papillae → capillaries → sensory receptors.
🔻
Reticular dermis → dense irregular connective tissue → collagen + elastic fibers → most skin appendages.
🔻
Dermal blood vessels → supply tissues + participate in thermoregulation.
✔️
Dermis = support + strength + sensation + vascular supply + temperature regulation
🎯 7. Sensory Receptors of the Skin
✨ A. Overview of Skin Sensory Receptors
🔻
The skin contains specialized sensory receptors that allow the nervous system to detect changes in the external environment and at the body surface.
🔻
These receptors detect different types of stimuli, including touch, pressure, vibration, pain, temperature, itching, and tissue deformation.
🔻
Skin receptors can be broadly classified into non-capsulated receptors and encapsulated receptors.
✔️
Skin receptors = sensory structures that detect touch, pressure, pain, temperature, vibration, and other stimuli
✨ B. Non-Capsulated (Simple) Receptors
🔻
Non-capsulated receptors do not have a specialized connective-tissue capsule surrounding their sensory endings.
✨ 1. Tactile Discs (Merkel Discs)
🔻
Merkel discs consist of sensory nerve endings associated with Merkel cells located in the stratum basale of the epidermis.
🔻
They function as mechanoreceptors, responding to mechanical deformation of the skin.
🔻
They are especially important for detecting light touch and fine details, helping the nervous system distinguish small differences in the surface being touched.
✔️
Merkel discs = light touch + fine tactile discrimination
✨ 2. Free Nerve Endings
🔻
Free nerve endings are simple sensory nerve endings that extend into the lower epidermis and papillary dermis.
🔻
They are widely distributed throughout the skin.
🔻
Different free nerve endings detect different stimuli, including pain, temperature, itching, and some forms of touch.
🔻
They are particularly important for detecting potentially harmful stimuli and changes in environmental temperature.
✔️
Free nerve endings = pain + temperature + itching + touch
✨ 3. Hair Root Plexus
🔻
The hair root plexus is a network of sensory nerve fibers surrounding the base of a hair follicle.
🔻
Movement of the hair bends or distorts the surrounding receptor endings.
🔻
This allows the nervous system to detect hair movement and very light contact with the skin.
✔️
Hair root plexus = hair movement + light touch
✨ C. Encapsulated Receptors
🔻
Encapsulated receptors contain sensory nerve endings surrounded by specialized connective-tissue structures.
🔻
These receptors are particularly important for different forms of mechanical sensation, including fine touch, pressure, vibration, and tissue deformation.
✨ 1. Tactile Corpuscles (Meissner Corpuscles)
🔻
Meissner corpuscles are small, oval or elliptical encapsulated receptors located within the dermal papillae.
🔻
They are especially numerous in highly sensitive areas such as the fingertips, palms, soles, lips, eyelids, and other specialized regions.
🔻
Their sensory endings are arranged within the capsule and respond to mechanical deformation.
🔻
They are specialized for light, fine, and discriminatory touch.
🔻
They are particularly useful for detecting subtle changes when an object moves across the skin.
✔️
Meissner corpuscles = light touch + fine tactile discrimination
✨ 2. Lamellated (Pacinian) Corpuscles
🔻
Pacinian corpuscles are large, oval-shaped encapsulated receptors with a characteristic onion-like arrangement of concentric lamellae surrounding a central sensory axon.
🔻
They are located deep within the reticular dermis and hypodermis and can also occur around structures such as ligaments, joint capsules, and mesenteries.
🔻
Their deep location makes them especially sensitive to mechanical forces transmitted through deeper tissues.
🔻
They detect deep pressure, sustained touch, tension, and high-frequency vibration.
✔️
Pacinian corpuscles = deep pressure + vibration + mechanical deformation
✨ 3. Ruffini Corpuscles
🔻
Ruffini corpuscles are elongated or spindle-shaped encapsulated receptors located mainly in the deeper dermis.
🔻
They are associated with collagenous connective tissue and respond when the surrounding tissue is stretched or deformed.
🔻
They detect continuous pressure and tissue distortion.
🔻
They also contribute to the perception of skin stretch and sustained mechanical forces.
✨ 4. Krause End Bulbs
🔻
Krause end bulbs are small, delicate encapsulated sensory structures.
🔻
They are found particularly in specialized areas such as the conjunctiva of the eye and mucosa of the oropharynx.
🔻
They have traditionally been associated with detection of pressure and low-frequency vibration.
✔️
Krause end bulbs = pressure + low-frequency vibration
✨ D. High-Yield Comparison
🔻
Merkel discs → light touch and fine tactile discrimination
🔻
Free nerve endings → pain, temperature, itching, and touch
🔻
Hair root plexus → hair movement and light touch
🔻
Meissner corpuscles → light, fine touch
🔻
Pacinian corpuscles → deep pressure and high-frequency vibration
🔻
Ruffini corpuscles → sustained pressure and tissue stretch
🔻
Krause end bulbs → pressure and low-frequency vibration
✨ E. Functional Organization
🔻
Different receptors are specialized for different forms of mechanical and environmental stimulation.
🔻
Superficial receptors, such as Merkel discs and Meissner corpuscles, are especially important for detecting fine and light touch.
🔻
Deep receptors, particularly Pacinian and Ruffini corpuscles, are more important for detecting pressure, vibration, and tissue deformation.
🔻
Free nerve endings provide important protective sensations such as pain and temperature.
✔️
Superficial = fine touch | Deep = pressure/vibration/stretch | Free endings = pain & temperature
🎯 8. Histology of Skin Appendages (Adnexa)
✨ A. Hairs (Pili) & Hair Follicles
🔻
Hair is made of hard keratin, which is tougher and more compact than the keratin of the epidermis.
🔻
The hair shaft has three concentric layers:
1. Medulla → innermost core, composed of loosely arranged keratinized cells with air spaces.
2. Cortex → middle and thickest layer, containing keratinized and often pigmented cells; it gives hair most of its strength and color.
3. Cuticle → outermost layer, formed by overlapping, scale-like cells that protect the inner layers.
🔻
The hair follicle surrounds the hair root and extends downward into the dermis and sometimes the hypodermis.
🔻
Important follicular structures include:
Connective tissue sheath → outer dermal covering containing collagen fibers.
Glassy membrane → thickened basement membrane separating the connective tissue sheath from the epithelial root sheath.
External epithelial root sheath → continuation of the epidermis surrounding the follicle.
Internal epithelial root sheath → surrounds the developing hair and includes Henle's layer and Huxley's layer.
🔻
The expanded base of the follicle is the hair bulb.
🔻
The hair matrix contains rapidly dividing cells that produce the hair shaft and internal root sheath.
🔻
The hair papilla is a vascular connective-tissue projection into the hair bulb that supplies nutrients and signals to the matrix.
✨ Hair Types
🔻
Lanugo → fine, soft fetal hair present during late fetal development.
🔻
Vellus hair → fine, short, lightly pigmented or unpigmented hair covering much of the body.
🔻
Terminal hair → thicker, longer, and usually pigmented hair found on areas such as the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes, and, after puberty, the axillary and pubic regions.
✔️
Hair = medulla + cortex + cuticle, produced by the hair matrix within the follicle.
✨ B. Nails
🔻
Nails are plates of tightly packed dead keratinized cells containing hard keratin.
🔻
They protect the distal ends of the fingers and toes and assist with fine manipulation.
✨ Main Nail Structures
🔻
Nail root → proximal portion embedded beneath the skin fold.
🔻
Nail matrix → region containing actively dividing cells responsible for nail growth.
🔻
Nail plate/body → visible hard portion of the nail resting on the nail bed.
🔻
Nail bed → tissue beneath the nail plate, consisting mainly of the stratum basale and stratum spinosum.
🔻
Eponychium (cuticle) → extension of the stratum corneum from the proximal nail fold onto the nail plate.
🔻
Hyponychium → thickened epidermis beneath the free distal edge of the nail.
🔻
Lunula → pale, crescent-shaped region near the nail root produced by the relatively thick underlying matrix.
🔻
Nail growth results from continuous cell division in the nail matrix, followed by keratinization.
✔️
Nail matrix = growth center of the nail.
✨ C. Cutaneous Glands
✨ 1. Sebaceous Glands
🔻
Sebaceous glands are simple branched alveolar/acinar glands.
🔻
They usually open into hair follicles and are generally absent from the palms and soles.
🔻
Their secretion is called sebum, an oily lipid-rich substance that helps lubricate and protect the skin and hair.
🔻
Sebaceous glands use holocrine secretion: cells accumulate lipids, then break down and release their contents.
🔻
Some sebaceous glands are modified and do not open into hair follicles, including areolar glands of Montgomery and tarsal (Meibomian) glands.
✔️
Sebaceous glands → holocrine secretion → sebum → lubrication and protection.
✨ 2. Eccrine (Merocrine) Sweat Glands
🔻
Eccrine glands are simple coiled tubular glands and are widely distributed throughout the skin.
🔻
They are especially numerous on the palms, soles, and forehead.
🔻
Their ducts open directly onto the skin surface.
✨ Secretory Cells
🔻
Clear cells → contribute water and electrolytes to sweat.
🔻
Dark cells → produce glycoprotein-rich secretory material and contribute to local defense.
🔻
Myoepithelial cells → contract around the secretory portion and help move secretion into the duct.
🔻
Eccrine glands are primarily controlled by sympathetic cholinergic fibers.
🔻
Their major function is thermoregulation through evaporation of sweat from the skin surface.
✔️
Eccrine glands → sweat → cooling of the body.
✨ 3. Apocrine Sweat Glands
🔻
Apocrine glands are large coiled tubular glands with relatively wide lumens.
🔻
They are concentrated mainly in the axillary and anogenital regions and become functionally active around puberty.
🔻
Their ducts usually empty into hair follicles rather than directly onto the skin surface.
🔻
Despite their name, human apocrine glands release their secretion mainly by merocrine exocytosis.
🔻
Their secretion is relatively viscous and protein-rich.
🔻
They are activated mainly by sympathetic adrenergic stimulation, particularly during emotional stress and other stimuli.
🔻
They are not primarily involved in thermoregulation.
✨ Modified Apocrine Glands
🔻
Ceruminous glands → produce components of cerumen (earwax) in the external auditory canal.
🔻
Glands of Moll → modified sweat glands associated with the eyelid margin.
✔️
Apocrine glands → specialized secretion + hair follicles + activity increases after puberty.
🎯 9. High-Yield Clinical & Pathological Correlations
✨ A. Skin Malignancies
🔻
Skin cancers are abnormal proliferations of cells within the skin. The major types discussed here are basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and malignant melanoma.
✨ 1. Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)
🔻
Origin: BCC arises from cells associated with the stratum basale.
🔻
It is the most common skin cancer and is generally the least aggressive of the three major types.
🔻
Histologically, it shows nests and cords of basaloid cells that proliferate downward from the epidermis into the underlying tissue.
🔻
Location: It commonly develops on sun-exposed areas, especially the face and neck.
🔻
BCC is usually slow-growing and has a low tendency to metastasize, but untreated lesions can invade and damage surrounding tissues.
✔️
BCC = basal cells + slow growth + local tissue invasion + rare metastasis.
✨ 2. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
🔻
Origin: SCC develops from keratinocytes, particularly those associated with the stratum spinosum.
🔻
It is less common than BCC but is more capable of invasion and metastasis.
🔻
Histologically, malignant squamous cells proliferate through the epidermis and may invade the dermis.
🔻
The tumor may show abnormal keratin production and cellular atypia.
🔻
Location: It frequently occurs on chronically sun-exposed skin, although it can develop elsewhere.
🔻
SCC may spread to regional lymph nodes if it becomes invasive.
✔️
SCC = squamous keratinocytes + dermal invasion + greater metastatic potential than BCC.
✨ 3. Malignant Melanoma
🔻
Origin: Malignant melanoma arises from melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the epidermis.
🔻
